rows.decision: Use native Foundry application and form styling rather than a Regionwright-specific imitation theme.
rows.next_review: Review only if Foundry changes its application/form contract.
rows.rationale: The interface should remain familiar and automatically follow Foundry theme behavior and control states.

rows.decision: Use separate roll and Hunt windows and force immediate normal-only D&D5e skill checks.
rows.next_review: Review after live v0.3.0 playtest.
rows.rationale: The player should see and understand the roll result without an extra configuration window, while the shooting game should have a clean dedicated surface.

rows.decision: Zero the Hunting Bow around normal hunting range and keep gravity as a trajectory input beyond the zero.
rows.next_review: Tune zero range only from live shot feel.
rows.rationale: Raw horizontal-launch gravity produced visually excessive drop at 35 yards; a sighted launch preserves realistic angle/drop while matching how an aimed bow is used.

rows.decision: Use RK4 numerical integration with source-calibrated quadratic drag and practical multi-distance sight references instead of hand-tuned drop values.
rows.next_review: Tune equipment parameters only from live play or better equipment-specific measurements.
rows.rationale: Published archery physics provides a defensible trajectory model and avoids repeated subjective tuning of gravity/drop constants.

rows.decision: Use a nonlinear continuous tension curve rather than milestone pulses or discrete visual draw stages.
rows.next_review: Tune exponent/full-draw time from live play only.
rows.rationale: The desired impact comes from increasing resistance near full draw, not from making the entire draw slow or layering on arcade-style feedback.

rows.decision: Use force/work-inspired increasing resistance with pulse markers, not arbitrary ease-out timing.
rows.next_review: Tune full-draw time and starting resistance only from live play.
rows.rationale: The desired heavy-bow feel is progressively greater resistance toward full draw; useful milestone pulses should remain as timing feedback.

rows.decision: Make wind the principal visible aiming correction and remove automatic crosshair sway.
rows.next_review: Review wind severity later as part of hunt difficulty profiles.
rows.rationale: Wind creates readable player-controlled compensation; involuntary reticle movement caused discomfort and added little gameplay value.

rows.decision: Use a smooth back-loaded time curve so the first half is fast, the middle slows sharply, and the final quarter crawls to full draw.
rows.next_review: Tune full draw time or curve constants only from live play.
rows.rationale: The prior physically inspired work curve was still too fast through the middle and did not communicate the desired heavy-bow resistance in play.

rows.decision: Use smooth walking plus stationary shooting windows, and make movement affect arrow-arrival hit geometry.
rows.next_review: Tune movement speed and pause duration from live play.
rows.rationale: This turns the accepted slow heavy-bow draw into an anticipation/timing mechanic without reintroducing involuntary reticle movement.

rows.decision: Use visible exertion-weighted stamina as a finite hold resource and auto-lower the bow at exhaustion.
rows.next_review: Tune drain/recovery rates from live play.
rows.rationale: Moving quarry plus a long heavy draw creates meaningful timing only if holding indefinitely has a visible opportunity cost, without reintroducing uncomfortable aim movement.

rows.decision: Back-load arrow velocity against continuous draw strength while keeping the existing full-draw reference speed.
rows.next_review: Tune minimum speed or exponent only from live play.
rows.rationale: Live play showed the old sublinear curve made partial and full shots too similar in flight time. Strong speed separation makes draw timing matter against moving quarry.

rows.decision: Derive partial-draw arrow speed from normalized stored bow energy instead of tuning a standalone draw-speed exponent.
rows.next_review: Review only if the draw curve or full-draw bow calibration changes.
rows.rationale: This unifies the accepted draw-resistance curve with projectile speed through force/work and kinetic-energy relationships while preserving the validated full-draw trajectory.

rows.decision: Use a linear force-draw approximation with quadratic cumulative work/time and a 2.5-second full draw.
rows.next_review: Revisit total draw duration only with better measured heavy-warbow kinematic evidence.
rows.rationale: The earlier fourth-power curve was intentionally dramatic for gameplay, but research supports a much closer-to-linear force rise for a heavy self bow.

rows.decision: Synchronize visual projectile motion to physics and provide a restrained movement-only dynamic lead reference plus tracer feedback.
rows.next_review: Tune lead-cue visibility only after live play.
rows.rationale: Moving shots should be difficult because of real timing and compensation, not because the rendered arrow/deer timeline differs from hit-resolution physics.

rows.decision: Use a tiny invisible horizontal collision forgiveness window for correct-direction near-miss leads and remove the visible predictor.
rows.next_review: Tune only from live moving-target play.
rows.rationale: Skyrim-like feel appears to come partly from hidden combat aim correction; visible prediction was not intuitive in live play.

rows.decision: Temporarily remove wind from live Hunting until arrow drop is accepted.
rows.next_review: Re-enable wind only after drop calibration is accepted.
rows.rationale: Isolating gravity/drop removes a confounding variable while tuning projectile feel.

rows.decision: Use accelerating stamina depletion and red UI pulse rather than camera/reticle shake; use green draw milestone pulses.
rows.next_review: Tune drain cap and pulse thresholds from live play only.
rows.rationale: This conveys increasing physical struggle without reintroducing motion that caused vertigo and aligns positive/negative feedback colors.

rows.decision: Diagnose live bow calibration with a deterministic lab and unified projectile simulation before changing gravity, drag, velocity, or aiming model.
rows.next_review: After live lab testing choose final live profile/aiming model.
rows.rationale: Research shows current architecture is sound but current modern-reference constants and automatic pin sight may be inappropriate for the intended heavy self-bow feel.

rows.decision: Guard the ResizeObserver target Element and skip observation when it is missing.

Do not fabricate clock puzzle setting, N3 branch unlock, U2 history interpretation or Founder Portrait stage; they remain governed open work.

Retain full immutable backup; ensure any future deletes have per-ID reviewed manifest, tested exact-ID restore and independent final verify. Use Tokens layer rather than Regions editing layer to conceal editing overlays without affecting gameplay.

Preserve the verified full backup as an inert recovery artifact; do not conduct archival or deletion without a new user request. Resume normal roadmap work.

Do not install or auto-trigger the candidates until there is an approved GM/story trigger, persistent one-shot state, exact asset provenance and an authorized executable contract verified on players; M1 clock cue stays blocked. No loud jump-scare or global light toggle merely on Region enter.

Use Scene-owned persistent m2HauntedPianoPlayed state, audience targeting, source hash/asset guards, and no automatic cue on entering a Region. rows.statement: The central project is DiceBox Campaign Helper: a semantic campaign compiler, runtime, and Foundry VTT bridge with an associated Foundry module.
rows.title: Central project identity

rows.statement: Stable DiceBox Campaign Helper IDs are canonical identity; Foundry _id, UUID, names, paths, and file names are runtime bindings only.
rows.title: Semantic identity

rows.statement: Campaign Assistant/DiceBox semantic specifications are authoritative; Foundry documents, images, Regions, Activities, and module state are compiled projections or runtime bindings.
rows.title: Projection boundary

rows.statement: AI intent must pass trust classification, live reconnaissance, capability resolution, schema/reference/authority checks, sovereignty checks, dry run, transaction, read-back, postcondition verification, and receipt/recovery.
rows.title: Mutation pipeline

rows.statement: Player-triggered protected mutations route to an active authorized GM/executor; privilege elevation transfers execution, not permission.
rows.title: No direct player protected writes

rows.statement: During play, runtime state is sovereign. Rebuilds preserve HP, resources, positions, effects, combat chronology, player/GM changes, foreign content, and moved/destroyed furnishing unless an explicit reviewed repair is requested.
rows.title: Runtime sovereignty

rows.statement: Use native Foundry/D&D5e primitives when semantically complete and exact-stack eligible; optional modules and macros are capability-gated adapters.
rows.title: Native first

rows.statement: Exactly one subsystem owns each mechanic; presentation systems never become mechanical authority.
rows.title: One mechanical owner

rows.statement: DiceBox preserves Utility and Use as separate semantic categories even if D&D5e 5.3.3 exposes only the utility runtime type.
rows.title: Utility versus Use

rows.statement: For D&D5e mechanics, prefer native Activity, then Midi resolution/composition, then Effects/DAE, Region/Scene, and only then an Additional Activity or macro for an uncovered verb.
rows.title: Activity-first compiler

rows.statement: Midi-QOL owns resolution workflow such as targeting, attack/save/damage adjudication, reactions, effects, OverTime, cleanup, and undo where supported; Activities express the action.
rows.title: Midi role

rows.statement: DAE is an optional extension to native Active Effects; DAE lifecycle callbacks are effect-state behavior, while Midi macros are transient Activity workflow behavior.
rows.title: DAE role

rows.statement: Scene Regions contain geometry, embedded Behaviors, and event subscriptions; Regionwright/DMF provide explicit selection, owned reconciliation, reset, and capability gating.
rows.title: Region authority

rows.statement: Physical geometry, topology, clearance, anchors, and relationships exist before pixels; image output and Foundry placeables are projections from the same blueprint.
rows.title: Spatial Blueprint

rows.statement: Generated images cannot define topology, scale, exact text, puzzle logic, furnishing mechanics, or Foundry rules. Approved bytes are reused by hash during normal rebuilds.
rows.title: Images are renderers

rows.statement: The KB is layered into canonical contracts, project dossiers, campaign packs, historical conversations, evidence, trials, and implementation contracts.
rows.title: Knowledge base layering

rows.statement: DiceBox creation targets Foundry 14.367 Stable 9 and D&D5e 5.3.3; Midi, DAE, SocketLib, and other modules are optional exact-stack capabilities.
rows.title: Target stack

rows.statement: Successful import, static tests, or a successful chat response is not Ready-to-Play; certification needs exact environment, actual document use, player-role, recovery, and blocker evidence.
rows.title: Readiness evidence

rows.statement: Regionwright passes 114 deterministic tests, but live module discovery, canvas selection, real native behavior write/reset, event context, and fresh two-client proof remain required.
rows.title: Regionwright current evidence

rows.statement: Dungeon Master's Forge verification passes with zero failures/warnings and reports 274 AI-service plus 168 module tests, but static/isolated evidence does not establish full in-world functionality.
rows.title: DMF current evidence

rows.statement: Region Editor is largely untracked and DMF is a dirty tester workspace; neither should be cleaned, reset, or treated as an immutable release source without explicit snapshotting.
rows.title: Source hygiene

rows.statement: Iggwilv Tower, Prime Arachnid, puzzle names, authored UUIDs, and exact campaign topology remain campaign/project packs, not global DiceBox rules.
rows.title: Campaign scope boundary

rows.statement: The linked Campaign Assistant project records Research #1-#40 complete/closed, while targeted deepening and implementation/certification studies remain separately tracked.
rows.title: Numbered research status

rows.statement: Every research pass or sub-pass must update the research master, machine-readable status, source index, and trial ledger, and state the exact next continuation point.
rows.title: Research self-update rule

rows.statement: A Scene is not a map image; it is a compiled environment containing dimensions, grid, Levels, placeables, links, environment, navigation, and initial view.
rows.title: Scene is compiled environment

rows.statement: Campaign-critical maps require authoritative spatial blueprint and deterministic graybox review before expensive image generation.
rows.title: Graybox before artwork

rows.statement: Generated automation must be declarative, bounded, reviewed, exact-artifact tested, and free of eval/new Function/arbitrary remote code or raw database access.
rows.title: No generated arbitrary code

rows.statement: Create and verify destination documents before writing links, use exact UUID/runtime bindings, detect stale links, and guard against loops/bounce.
rows.title: Two-pass linked creation

rows.statement: Normal rebuilds reuse approved media by immutable hash; regeneration is explicit, provenance-aware, and validated for rights, dimensions, topology, alpha, and distribution.
rows.title: Approved asset reuse

rows.statement: Effects, Regions, audio, Tiles, and module state are projections or runtime state; quest and campaign knowledge truth remains in the DiceBox state model.
rows.title: Campaign truth versus runtime projection

rows.statement: Foundry requires a root module.json whose id matches the module directory; ES modules, compatibility, relationships, manifest, and download metadata are package concerns from the first module slice.
rows.title: Module manifest boundary

rows.statement: Foundry modifyBatch can prevent partial commit for supported operations but cannot reference an ID created earlier within the same batch; dependent creation requires staged transactions.
rows.title: Batch limitation

rows.statement: An FTS5 external/content index must remain synchronized with source rows; the current DiceBox KB is compiled from schema and seed and does not assume live editing.
rows.title: FTS rebuild boundary

rows.statement: D&D5e exposes Activity lifecycle hooks, but DiceBox must inspect the actual registered Activity classes/hooks on the exact target runtime before capability promotion.
rows.title: Activity hook boundary

rows.statement: The M0 checkout contains four package boundaries, canonical schemas, a readiness-gated read-only bridge, and a no-op Foundry manifest/bootstrap; it does not claim live runtime or world-mutation evidence.
rows.title: M0 contract spine

rows.statement: A standalone D&D5e Player Turn Coach competes with current Foundry HUDs, player-authored reminders, manual action tracking, and turn analytics; contextual ranking should remain a supporting feature rather than the first product thesis.
rows.title: Action HUD competition boundary

rows.statement: Campaign Continuity / Session Rescue is the current product finalist because it targets GM-paid disruption costsâ€”absent players, off-script play, and uncertain resumptionâ€”while reusing semantic state, provenance, staging, read-back, and recovery assets. It remains unvalidated until behavioral buyer evidence exists.
rows.title: Session Rescue finalist

rows.statement: Foundry package snapshots and current document backup modules restore whole packages or named documents, while campaign-planning and AI co-pilot tools cover preparation or continuation. The research found no directly comparable current package advertising a typed session branch with selective semantic merge/discard; this absence is a research hypothesis, not proof of uniqueness.
rows.title: Semantic branch gap

rows.statement: Foundry can support a previewable branch using serializable Document data, local validation, and supported create/update operations, but cross-document atomicity is not universal. Roll20 live Mods are creator/Pro-bound and Fantasy Grounds uses XML campaign state plus Lua/XML extensions; portability should therefore begin with read-only neutral branch packets and explicit adapters.
rows.title: Neutral branch packet boundary

rows.statement: Foundry supports one-time premium modules, but Safe Mode is episodic and competes with free backups, notes, and planning tools. The most plausible buyer is a GM with persistent or paid weekly play; pricing should test a free checkpoint/export plus a $15â€“25 one-time protection layer. This is a falsifiable hypothesis, not observed purchase conversion.
rows.title: Willingness-to-pay hypothesis

rows.statement: Foundry backups, Recycle Bin, World CLI, Campaign Forge, and manual duplicate-world workflows cover adjacent recovery, live-edit, and campaign-state jobs. Campaign Safe Mode is defensible only if a typed session branch with semantic diff and selective merge/discard solves a real table decision better than those alternatives.
rows.title: Safety moat is insufficient

rows.statement: Players report overloaded sheets, unintuitive rolls, stale or broken sheet state, onboarding difficulty, mobile/second-screen needs, and accessibility barriers. Current Foundry packages already cover much of the generic companion, mobile, navigation, inventory, and trading space, so player pain alone does not establish a new paid category.
rows.title: Player friction is real but saturated

rows.statement: Because VTTs expose different live-state and permission boundaries, cross-VTT portability should begin with a neutral read-only session packet and player-safe re-entry view. Foundry can be the first live adapter; universal live synchronization remains out of scope until explicit adapters prove equivalent behavior.
rows.title: Neutral session packet is the portability wedge

rows.statement: Campaign Safe Mode is useful but is not naturally attention-grabbing in a marketplace where visual content and immediate player-facing outcomes dominate browsing. It must be presented as Campaign Continuity: a visible disruption-to-branch-to-merge outcome, not as generic safety infrastructure.
rows.title: Safe Mode has an invisible-insurance problem

rows.statement: The candidate should be tested with a five-second thumbnail/clip and a thirty-second silent demo. It passes attention only if qualified GMs can identify the user, moment, and payoff and prefer it over a real backup, journal, or duplicate-world alternative.
rows.title: Desirability must be demonstrated without explanation

rows.statement: A visible campaign timeline, current branch lane, Keep/Discard semantic diff, player-safe Re-entry Card, and Canonize action can make Campaign Continuity glanceable while remaining grounded in the branch engine. It is not a validated product surface and must not degrade into a prettier recap or wiki.
rows.title: Canon and Branch Board is the hero-artifact hypothesis

rows.statement: Absent-player and off-script problems can cause cancelled sessions, one-shots, ghosted characters, or campaign momentum loss, but groups often have workable social alternatives. The pain is not yet sufficient evidence for a paid branch product.
rows.title: Disruption pain is real but continuity purchase urgency is mixed

rows.statement: Update, migration, and data-loss failures create sharper game-night urgency and support a self-contained launchable save-state/preflight concept. Free Foundry backups, Recycle Bin, World CLI, and manual copies remain credible alternatives, so the challenger requires direct buyer comparison.
rows.title: Campaign Guardian is a stronger urgency challenger but not a clear winner

rows.statement: Foundry and Forge cover most save-state recovery, Battle Replay covers visual combat replay, and current modules cover encounter generation, improvisation, progressive events, and cinematic scene control. These should be treated as adjacent features or explicit alternatives, not new product directions.
rows.title: Guardian, Replay, and improvisation suites are not standalone gaps

rows.statement: The remaining candidate is a typed branch across campaign state and non-combat Documents with player/GM visibility boundaries, selective merge, provenance, and recovery receipts. No current evidence proves buyers will pay for it, so it remains a testable hypothesis rather than a market conclusion.
rows.title: Semantic non-combat selective canonization remains the narrow gap hypothesis

rows.statement: Foundry v14 exposes serializable Document source data, ephemeral clone, local update/validation, permission checks, create/update operations, and pre/post update hooks. These primitives are sufficient for a read-only checkpoint, preview diff, and GM-authorized staged merge prototype.
rows.title: Foundry API supports a narrow branch prototype

rows.statement: Differential updates, array replacement, staged dependent creation, module-owned state, external media, and cross-document failures prevent an assumption of atomic rollback. The implementation needs dependency ordering, idempotent receipts, authoritative reread, compensating recovery, and explicit unsupported-state handling.
rows.title: Foundry does not provide universal transaction or state coverage

rows.statement: The current Foundry package index lists thousands of add-on modules and more than a thousand premium packages. Current product pages that compete for attention lead with screenshots, video, modern UI, or an immediate player-visible outcome. This establishes an attention standard, not a sales ranking.
rows.title: Foundry paid-product browse is visual and crowded

rows.statement: Safe Mode is invisible infrastructure for an episodic problem; Undo the Session creates retcon/trust concerns; Continue After a Disruption is clear but not immediately visual. Canon & Branch Board may be attractive but overlaps with current campaign dashboards, timelines, clue boards, and organizer surfaces.
rows.title: Campaign Continuity fails the first storefront attention hypothesis

rows.statement: A short ready-to-run, player-visible session can show its value in a listing through scenes, handouts, reveals, bounded choices, and a finished evening. It offers a clearer GM payer, recurring capsule purchases, and a neutral content/export boundary, but it remains unvalidated and competes with premium adventures and map/content packs.
rows.title: Adventure Capsules is the next product candidate

rows.statement: Current Foundry packages already offer minimal-prep, drop-in, one-session, animated, branching, and high-production adventures. This validates that GMs buy prepared content in principle, but it does not validate a new generic capsule.
rows.title: Ready-to-run Foundry adventure content is a real paid category but is crowded

rows.statement: Drop-in Dungeons, Prepared! 2, Dragonshorn, Boss Loot, Rultmoork, and premium publishers already cover ready-to-run maps, handouts, music, choices, adjustable difficulty, and Foundry integration. Branching tools such as UO Scenario Branches and Visual Novel Maker further reduce the feature gap.
rows.title: Generic Adventure Capsules have no sufficient competitive gap

rows.statement: A 60â€“120 minute no-canon session for variable attendance could target a recurring GM problem: preserving the scheduled social event when one or more players are absent without preparing or mutating the main campaign. This is only a hypothesis and must beat cancellation, ghosting, free PDFs, second worlds, and existing premium adventures in a real purchase-choice test.
rows.title: Adaptive Drop-In Capsules are the narrowed candidate

rows.statement: The local machine contains Foundry 14.367, D&D5e 5.3.3, a readable regionwright-testmap fixture manifest, DiceBox Campaign Helper 0.1.2, and optional Midi-QOL/DAE manifests.
rows.title: Exact target Foundry runtime is locally available

rows.statement: The read-only preflight passed data path, world identity, Foundry version, D&D5e version, DiceBox package, and optional module manifest checks, but returned BLOCKED because the ready-hook/live probe was NOT_TESTED.
rows.title: Manifest preflight does not certify live runtime behavior

rows.statement: The official Marketplace reports 1,227 products, 107 creators, 60,000 users, and 371 customer reviews after its first year, with filters for price, rating, publisher, tags, and verified version. This proves a meaningful discovery surface and a trust/attention burden, not product-level sales.
rows.title: Foundry premium discovery is large but attention-constrained

rows.statement: Omnipresence explicitly supports keeping characters, journals, and hotbars synchronized across Foundry worlds and names one-shot campaigns as a use case. A new product cannot differentiate on cross-world character continuity alone; it must sell the finished attendance-rescue experience and clean return.
rows.title: Omnipresence closes part of the Adaptive Drop-In gap

rows.statement: The trigger-based promise â€œOne player canceled. Donâ€™t cancel the game.â€ makes the Adaptive Drop-In Capsule more immediately legible than Safe Mode or Campaign Continuity. It remains a hypothesis until qualified buyers choose it over cancellation, a free PDF, a premium one-shot, a second world, or no purchase.
rows.title: Game Night Rescue is the sharper front-door message

rows.statement: A visual capsule alone is another ready-made adventure, while the branch engine alone is invisible infrastructure. The provisional paid unit is an original 60â€“120 minute capsule plus present-player selection, explicit no-canon status, safe exit, and player-safe return packet; Campaign Continuity remains reusable backend infrastructure.
rows.title: The storefront product must be content plus workflow

rows.statement: Foundry recommends Adventure Compendium Packs for complicated premium content, and its current AI policy requires prepared user-facing text, media, and marketing materials for official listings to originate from human creative work. A rights-clean original capsule is therefore a safer product path than an automatically generated content catalog.
rows.title: Official distribution adds rights and marketing constraints

rows.statement: Community reports show real absences and cancellations, but many home tables solve them with quorum rules, background characters, backup pilots, duplicate worlds, free one-shots, or rescheduling. The event is common enough to research but not yet a mass-market paid problem.
rows.title: Home-table attendance pain has low default willingness to pay

rows.statement: Published professional-GM offerings sell recurring sessions per player, packages, or booked events and may bill late cancellations or lose booking value. This gives Game Night Rescue a measurable ROI hypothesis around protecting prep, revenue, retention, and scheduled play, but does not prove module purchase intent.
rows.title: Paid and organized GMs have the clearest economic buyer case

rows.statement: Oronder explicitly targets West Marches and single-party campaigns with Discord access, scheduling, and cross-world character support. The remaining candidate must sell the finished no-canon session and safe exit rather than generic scheduling or synchronization.
rows.title: West Marches and rotating hosts are attractive but already served operationally

rows.statement: The strongest untested message is â€œProtect the booked game night when attendance changes,â€ aimed at paid/professional GMs and high-variance organizers. Home GMs remain useful for usability evidence, but their reactions cannot establish willingness to pay for the product.
rows.title: Game Night Rescue should be tested first with a payer-specific message

rows.statement: The local DMF project accepts natural-language item requests, compiles native D&D5e item specifications, repairs known schema/activity/targeting/resource/effect/summon issues, presents review findings, and attaches capability-gated Midi-QOL, DAE, or Item Macro routes when supported.
rows.title: DMF is an end-to-end item and automation compiler

rows.statement: D&D Item Auto Maker publicly emphasizes plain-English item generation and fully-statted Foundry documents with JSON export, while DMF additionally targets cross-module automation compilation and verification. This is a differentiation hypothesis, not buyer proof.
rows.title: DMF has a credible gap beyond plain-language item generation

rows.statement: Community requests show recurring difficulty wiring conditional damage, effects, charges, timing, Midi-QOL hooks, DAE, and Item Macro behavior. Simple-item GMs have cheaper alternatives, so broad willingness to pay remains unproven.
rows.title: The strongest DMF payer hypothesis is the automation-heavy D&D5e GM

rows.statement: â€œMake the homebrew item work, not just existâ€ presents DMF as a reviewed compiler that creates the item, explains dependencies, and supplies a verification receipt. It must beat native forms, Auto Maker, Item Creator, free macros, and community help.
rows.title: Custom Item Workshop is the buyer-facing DMF hypothesis

rows.statement: Reviewed item recipes, dependency declarations, assumptions, and verification receipts can be exported or re-rendered for another VTT, but Foundry Item documents and Midi-QOL hooks are platform-specific projections.
rows.title: DMF portability belongs at the recipe and receipt layer

rows.statement: The current D&D Item Auto Maker public package and source provide a short-description builder, direct world insertion, history/retry, JSON export, Patreon authentication, and monthly generation allowance. Its public surface does not advertise Midi-QOL/DAE/Item Macro wiring.
rows.title: Automaker establishes the direct-item speed baseline

rows.statement: Automaker is a credible baseline for simple items. DMF's defensible wedge is compiling and verifying the cross-module behavior of unusual items while preserving a fast core-only fallback.
rows.title: DMF should differentiate on automation completion, not basic generation speed

rows.statement: Automaker's source uses Patreon authentication and monthly generation allowances, showing a viable monetization design for an AI Foundry utility. No public evidence here establishes its conversion, retention, or revenue.
rows.title: Usage monetization is plausible but not sales proof

rows.statement: A side-by-side test must measure manual edits, module settings, working behavior, time to first usable item, and a real price choice. A simple generated core item is not enough to prove DMF value.
rows.title: The decisive DMF test is behavioral setup saved on a complex item

rows.statement: D&D5e Activities and the Item document model are Foundry/D&D5e-native. Midi-QOL, DAE, and Item Macro add Foundry-specific runtime behavior, so their compiled outputs cannot be treated as universal VTT artifacts.
rows.title: Foundry item automation is system-native

rows.statement: Roll20 Mod/API scripts are campaign-local and Pro-gated, while Fantasy Grounds uses built-in ruleset automation and separate XML/Lua extension or ruleset customization. Neither shares Foundry's document/module contract.
rows.title: Roll20 and Fantasy Grounds require separate projections

rows.statement: Intent, assumptions, activity/triggers, resource use, dependencies, unresolved clauses, approvals, test cases, and verification receipts can be exported neutrally even when runtime automation is platform-specific.
rows.title: The portable DMF boundary is a recipe and receipt

rows.statement: A neutral export may widen the buyer pool, but each live VTT projection multiplies capability, licensing, compatibility, and support work. Foundry automation must remain the reason to pay for the first release.
rows.title: Portability is a differentiator only if it does not dilute the Foundry wedge

rows.statement: A highly engaged current community discussion describes major releases as a gamble involving broken modules, changed workflows, stale documentation, and paid content that may become unusable until dependencies catch up. This is pain evidence, not purchase proof.
rows.title: Foundry upgrade breakage is a broad recurring GM pain

rows.statement: Foundry provides backups, snapshots, compatibility metadata, and package update controls. The unserved hypothesis is a world-specific report plus disposable clone and critical-path smoke tests that reveal behavioral failure before the live world is migrated.
rows.title: The upgrade gap is preflight and rehearsal, not backup alone

rows.statement: Module Compatibility Checker is old and metadata-oriented; Module Profiles, Module Loadouts, Settings Vault, and Content Backup & Restore preserve or restore state but do not rehearse a campaign's actual workflows on the candidate stack.
rows.title: Existing compatibility and configuration tools leave a behavior-testing gap

rows.statement: The promise â€œknow what will break before you updateâ€ addresses the GM responsible for an active campaign, produces a visible red/amber/green result, and recurs with core/system/module releases.
rows.title: Upgrade Guardian has a stronger ordinary-GM front door than DMF

rows.statement: Static metadata misses runtime breakage, and a disposable clone may not cover every workflow. The product must report observed, known, and untested areas and never turn a green result into a guarantee.
rows.title: Upgrade Guardian cannot honestly promise universal safety

rows.statement: The package/dependency/health-report abstraction can later support other plugin-rich VTTs, but live clone and smoke-test adapters will be platform-specific. Cross-VTT support is an extension path, not an initial promise.
rows.title: Upgrade safety is Foundry-first with a portable report model

rows.statement: A world-running module should not copy its own open database, replace the active Foundry executable, or claim to rehearse a future stack in place. A local companion can operate at setup time and launch a closed-world disposable rehearsal.
rows.title: Upgrade Guardian needs a local companion boundary

rows.statement: Package manifests expose compatibility, dependencies, and version history, while user-data and backup APIs provide the inputs for snapshots. These signals cannot prove that a selected campaign workflow will work after migration.
rows.title: Foundry metadata supports static preflight but not behavioral certification

rows.statement: Upgrade Guardian can inspect manifests and user-owned files, invoke the user's installed Foundry, and store local reports, but should not redistribute Foundry, paid modules, rulebook text, art, or campaign assets.
rows.title: The safe distribution boundary is user-owned installation inspection

rows.statement: A disposable clone may require disk space, closed processes, online entitlements, and copies of external module-owned state; unselected workflows remain untested. Reports need explicit metadata-compatible, probe-passed, probe-failed, not-exercised, and restore-verified states.
rows.title: Upgrade rehearsal has material false-confidence risks

rows.statement: The first product should not be a self-modifying in-world module or a cloud service. Its credible boundary is a Windows/local setup companion, disposable rehearsal world, optional Foundry probe, and evidence-labeled report viewer.
rows.title: Upgrade Guardian is a local companion plus optional probe

rows.statement: Foundry's pre-update compatibility check, built-in backups/snapshots, portable builds, and documented multi-version installation address the basic compatibility and recovery jobs. A new product cannot sell those capabilities alone.
rows.title: Foundry already covers generic pre-update compatibility and rollback

rows.statement: The Forge and VTT Online sell ongoing hosting with automatic backups and version choice, providing a paid alternative to self-managed runtime safety. Their existence is market evidence for the problem but also a direct competitive benchmark.
rows.title: Hosting services monetize operational risk reduction

rows.statement: GM test modes use DEER_TEST_HIT_ZONES for both visible anatomical overlay and hit/forgiveness classification, while production DEER_HIT_ZONES remain the default for normal Hunting.
rows.title: Hunting v0.3.24 isolated anatomical target is deployed

rows.statement: The anatomical target revision passes 304/304 Regionwright tests, source/dist and installed hashes match, and Foundry serves v0.3.24.
rows.title: Hunting v0.3.24 validation passed

rows.statement: The v2 process monitor is alive as PID 31352 and writing samples in session 20261004-172927-v2 while Foundry PID 22760 serves the test world.
rows.title: External crash monitor is armed for v0.3.24 live testing

rows.statement: The animated arrow/tracer finishes from the release-space projected trajectory while the impact marker is deer-local at the impact-time anatomy point, causing visible separation when quarry moves during flight.
rows.title: Arrow/tracer endpoint and impact marker currently use different coordinate spaces

rows.statement: v0.3.25 will derive the visual endpoint from the already-resolved impact-time deer position and hit point while leaving projectile simulation and classification unchanged.
rows.title: Impact visual synchronization must not alter hit physics

rows.statement: Quarry screen position now uses projectDeerCenterU with target-width pixels per metre, matching the arrow trajectory scale and eliminating the prior full-screen lane projection mismatch.
rows.title: Hunting v0.3.25 uses one physical screen projection for quarry and arrow

rows.statement: Automated tests prove that the arrow world endpoint and deer-local impact marker reduce to the same screen coordinate at 20, 45, and 65 yards while physics remains unchanged.
rows.title: Hunting v0.3.25 endpoint convergence is regression-tested

rows.statement: The visual synchronization revision passes 306/306 Regionwright tests, source/dist and installed hashes match, and the exact test world serves v0.3.25 under an active crash monitor.
rows.title: Hunting v0.3.25 validation passed

rows.statement: Community reports describe delaying upgrades during active campaigns, keeping an old version, or testing modules one at a time in a separate installation. This validates pain but supplies a low-cost workaround that a paid tool must beat.
rows.title: Many GMs solve upgrade risk by waiting or maintaining a manual test install

rows.statement: Core compatibility checks and backups reduce the novelty of a red/amber/green dashboard. The remaining purchase hypothesis is local per-world runtime locking, one-click known-good launch, and optional upgrade rehearsal for self-hosters or multi-world GMs.
rows.title: A generic Upgrade Guardian report is not yet a paid product

rows.statement: A one-time local price is credible only if self-hosters value control and reproducibility enough to reject low-cost hosting with version switching and snapshots. Price choice has not been observed.
rows.title: Campaign Runtime Locker must beat hosting and manual installs

rows.statement: Current community reports describe slow sheets, delayed chat, low frame rates, long-session degradation, and some players being unable to join or play. The reported causes span client hardware, browser/GPU settings, network conditions, asset load, chat size, scene complexity, and module interactions, so the symptom is visible while the cause is often unclear.
rows.title: Player-facing Foundry lag is recurring and difficult to localize

rows.statement: Axon's Performance Monitor provides live monitoring, scene/module diagnostics, benchmarks, reports, and recommendations; Performance Optimizer provides per-player profiles, GM controls, low-FPS warnings, and a benchmark; Prime Performance optimizes token UI rendering; and Find the Culprit automates module bisection. A generic FPS dashboard or optimizer would be a weak product.
rows.title: Foundry already has strong point solutions for performance

rows.statement: The checked tools expose metrics, apply client profiles, optimize a rendering path, or isolate modules. No evidence in this pass establishes a single product that correlates per-player FPS/latency/browser-GPU signals with scene assets, module events, and server timeline, then gives the GM a reproducible next action without blindly disabling half the world. This is a hypothesis, not a proven whitespace.
rows.title: The remaining performance gap is correlated incident diagnosis

rows.statement: The buyer-facing promise would be â€œFind who is lagging and why before game night,â€ followed by a short guided capture: identify affected clients, reproduce the symptom in a disposable or low-risk scene, correlate asset/module/browser signals, and produce a ranked action plan plus a reversible degraded-session profile.
rows.title: The eye-catching candidate is Session Health Autopsy

rows.statement: Players feel the pain, but the GM or host controls the module stack and is the person who loses session time, receives support requests, and decides whether to pay. A purchase case requires a recent incident that cost meaningful play time or threatened a session; general dislike of lag is not willingness-to-pay evidence.
rows.title: The likely payer is the GM responsible for a disrupted table

rows.statement: A neutral session-health record can represent client capability, scene/asset budget, event timestamps, latency/FPS samples, suspected cause, confidence, and recommended action. Collection and safe remediation remain VTT-specific because Foundry, Roll20, and other platforms expose different client and module boundaries.
rows.title: Performance evidence can have a portable report boundary

rows.statement: The first implementation should collect consented local/client metrics, avoid uploading raw chat or campaign content, support a disposable reproduction scene or read-only trace, label correlation as suspicion rather than proof, and apply only reversible profile changes. A â€œgreenâ€ performance result cannot certify every device or module combination.
rows.title: A credible diagnosis product must protect the live session

rows.statement: The category has active and recently updated competitors, so the product is not selected on the existence of lag alone. It remains worth a buyer test only if affected GMs prefer a guided cross-client diagnosis and reversible session profile over existing tools, support posts, module bisection, or simply asking players to lower settings.
rows.title: Generic performance tooling is rejected; guided incident response remains conditional

rows.statement: Foundry's own FAQ says mobile devices are not supported by the core software. Current community reports describe players on old laptops, phones, tablets, or unsupported browsers being unable to join or play, with screen sharing or a different VTT used as the fallback.
rows.title: Mobile and low-end player access is a real Foundry pain

rows.statement: Swipe VTT, Sheet Only, Foundry Tabletop Helpers, Companion Bridge/VTT Companion, and PocketScroll already offer some combination of touch controls, mobile sheets, chat, maps, combat, rolls, or GM controls. PocketScroll uses a GM subscription with free player invite links, while other products use free/core plus Patreon or premium features.
rows.title: The Foundry mobile companion category is already active

rows.statement: Roll20 retired its old mobile app in favor of a browser-first character experience and reports phone-ready D&D sheets with synchronized rolls/actions. This validates demand for a focused player surface but also creates a strong platform-level competitor for cross-VTT ambitions.
rows.title: Roll20 is investing in the same player-side direction

rows.statement: A new phone character sheet, touch map, or companion app would overlap multiple current offerings and would inherit app-store, authentication, system-adapter, and Foundry-version support costs. Mobile pain alone does not justify another paid companion.
rows.title: A generic mobile companion is a no-go

rows.statement: A narrower product could avoid full-canvas rendering and app installation: the GM shares a short invite, and an ordinary browser exposes the player's current character actions, rolls, chat, turn state, and a deliberately lightweight map/position view. It would need to beat PocketScroll's invite flow and existing mobile modules on device reach, setup, and resource use.
rows.title: Only a low-bandwidth browser relay remains a conditional wedge

rows.statement: Character summary, turn state, dice request, chat, and lightweight scene packets can be represented neutrally. Rules resolution, permissions, movement, effects, and inventory writes still require separate adapters for Foundry, Roll20, and other VTTs.
rows.title: A player-relay protocol is portable only at the action boundary

rows.statement: In a current Foundry companion discussion, players describe the wall of laptops and state that they would pay roughly â‚¬20â€“â‚¬25 for a useful phone experience; another participant names a lower one-time price as an immediate purchase. This is directional self-reported intent from one product thread, not representative conversion data.
rows.title: The mobile player problem has explicit non-zero price anchors

rows.statement: VTT Companion offers a â‚¬15 one-time Lifetime Link for its D&D5e premium module with optional subscriptions, while PocketScroll uses a GM subscription and free player invite links. These are evidence that a GM-paid, table-wide device utility can be monetized, not evidence of their sales or retention.
rows.title: Current companions demonstrate viable payment shapes

rows.statement: VTT Companion advertises a sub-5MB app, real-time sync, offline cached sheets, phone actions, Foundry v13/v14 support, and a one-time premium module. It also states that system-specific modules are needed for different systems. A new full mobile character app would have no obvious reason to win.
rows.title: The full mobile companion surface is already closed by a direct competitor

rows.statement: The companion discussion is driven by a concrete table problem: a GM projects the table while players need sheet interaction, and a laptop for every player crowds the physical table. The likely buyer is the GM who can buy one module for the group, while the player benefit supplies adoption pressure.
rows.title: Hybrid in-person groups are a visible payer segment

rows.statement: A defensible wedge would be a browser/PWA relay that avoids full Foundry canvas rendering and app-store installation, sends only current actions/rolls/chat/turn state plus a lightweight map or position view, and is designed for weak devices and low bandwidth. No checked evidence proves that this boundary beats the existing apps.
rows.title: The remaining candidate is a thin client, not a mobile companion

rows.statement: The observed one-time companion price and self-reported â‚¬20â€“â‚¬25 willingness-to-pay justify testing a GM-paid one-time range around â‚¬15, â‚¬20, and â‚¬25. They do not justify setting a final price or assuming that device reach is worth recurring payment.
rows.title: A first thin-client price test can use a â‚¬15â€“â‚¬25 GM-paid anchor

rows.statement: Foundry can remain the authority for permissions, Activities, Midi-QOL workflows, effects, movement, and inventory. The relay should send typed requests to the Foundry adapter and receive verified results; it should not duplicate rules or write directly from an untrusted player client.
rows.title: Thin-client feasibility depends on a bounded action gateway

rows.statement: The relay can operate on the user's running Foundry world and transmit only consented state needed for the active player view. It should not bundle D&D books, protected art, premium content, or a cloud copy of campaign data. Cross-VTT adapters would need their own capability and licensing review.
rows.title: A local-first relay can avoid content redistribution risk

rows.statement: The official module-development guidance allows a module to request a specialized socket namespace; the server relays arbitrary packets on module.{name} to connected clients. This supports a Foundry-mediated request/result channel, but does not by itself define a standalone browser client or its authentication.
rows.title: Foundry provides a module-scoped socket boundary

rows.statement: The v14 API documentation distinguishes a supported Public API from private or unclear surfaces and lists SocketInterface as the standardized helper for dispatching socket events. A product should stay within documented module, hook, socket, document, and permission boundaries and fail closed when a capability is unclear.
rows.title: The public API is safer than private client internals

rows.statement: Foundry separates role permissions from document permissions, and document ownership controls whether a user can view or edit particular Actors, Items, Journals, and other documents. A relay must authenticate as a Foundry user and project only the state that user may see; typed actions still require server-side capability and ownership checks.
rows.title: Foundry permissions can constrain relay-visible state and actions

rows.statement: Because Foundry is a self-hosted web framework with connected clients and a module socket boundary, a narrow relay could be delivered through the user's running Foundry instance without a separate cloud control plane. This is an architectural inference, not proof that an external PWA can join, authenticate, reconnect, or perform actions on the exact target stack.
rows.title: A local-first thin client is plausible but not yet proven as a separate PWA

rows.statement: Foundry's licensing guidance requires rights for included rules text, artwork, icons, music, and other distributed content; code that changes core behavior is generally a safer module boundary. The thin client should transmit consented live state from the customer's world rather than ship books, premium assets, or a hosted campaign copy.
rows.title: The relay must avoid republishing protected content

rows.statement: Foundry's module/socket/document model is not evidence that Roll20, Fantasy Grounds, or another VTT exposes the same runtime authority or permissions. A neutral player-action packet and receipt can be portable, while each live adapter must separately verify authentication, permissions, actions, and unsupported behavior.
rows.title: Cross-VTT portability belongs at the packet and capability layer

rows.statement: Current community reports describe players who still struggle after months with sheet tabs, targeting, icons, multiple action surfaces, and basic controls; some players report leaving or preferring a simpler VTT. Other users dispute the severity, so this is a recurring pain signal rather than universal demand.
rows.title: Foundry player friction includes repeated navigation and choice overload

rows.statement: Foundry Navigator provides keyboard-first and screen-reader-oriented navigation for D&D5e v13/v14; Accessibility Enhancements adds drag/drop alternatives and audio feedback; Stylish Action HUD provides party cards and quick actions; party-inventory tools simplify shared loot. A generic HUD or accessibility patch is therefore not an open product category.
rows.title: Existing packages cover slices of player-flow simplification

rows.statement: Recent player-friction reports describe multiple interfaces, HUD bloat, duplicate action locations, and uncertainty about which control is correct. The wedge must reduce visible choices and guide the next task rather than add another permanent toolbar.
rows.title: Adding another HUD can increase the problem it claims to solve

rows.statement: A per-player cockpit could show only the current task, legal/useful actions, relevant resources, target guidance, and a clear next step, with text labels and keyboard/screen-reader paths. It would hide irrelevant sheet surfaces and use Foundry as the authority instead of duplicating rules. No evidence yet proves it reduces table time or beats existing HUDs.
rows.title: Player Flow / Tabletop Ease Mode is a narrower alternate hypothesis

rows.statement: A GM can value fewer â€œwhere do I click?â€ interruptions, faster onboarding, and more independent players, but the current evidence is frustration and task failure rather than a price commitment. Buyer authority, session-frequency benefit, and non-zero price must be tested directly.
rows.title: The likely payer is the GM buying reduced table friction

rows.statement: A neutral task description such as choose action, choose target, confirm roll, spend resource, or resolve result could map to multiple VTTs. The UI, permissions, sheet schema, and live action execution remain platform- and system-specific.
rows.title: Player-flow portability is strongest at the task-graph layer

rows.statement: The candidate should demonstrate a confused player completing the next correct action without opening a full sheet or waiting for GM instructions. That â€œfrom stuck to playingâ€ moment is more legible than accessibility infrastructure, but it must be compared with existing HUDs and simple player training.
rows.title: The eye-catching promise is independent play, not another interface

rows.statement: The official Player Orientation tutorial covers joining, claiming characters, learning the interface, opening sheets, and moving on the map; the broader knowledge base and GM tutorials cover additional setup. A generic onboarding product must beat material that is already available at no extra cost.
rows.title: Foundry already provides a free player-onboarding baseline

rows.statement: Current community advice includes a dedicated learning session, a small tutorial campaign that introduces one module at a time, screen sharing, and existing HUDs or sheet simplification. These alternatives reduce the urgency for a standalone player-flow purchase.
rows.title: Groups commonly solve player confusion with instruction rather than purchase

rows.statement: The paid Pathfinder Beginner Box explicitly teaches both the game and Foundry features while delivering a complete adventure. This supports bundling onboarding into premium content, not pricing a generic player tutorial or cockpit by itself.
rows.title: Instruction can be monetized when bundled with valuable content

rows.statement: The research found recurring confusion and accessibility pain but no direct buyer price choice for a generic cockpit; free tutorials, training, existing HUDs, and simpler VTT alternatives are credible substitutes. Standalone product selection is therefore unsupported.
rows.title: Player Flow lacks direct willingness-to-pay evidence as a standalone product

rows.statement: Task graphs, contextual guidance, labels, keyboard paths, and result receipts remain valuable components for a thin relay or content product. They should not create a second standalone product scope unless a future buyer test produces direct payment evidence.
rows.title: Player Flow should remain a reusable feature boundary

rows.statement: Recent community discussions ask for better drawing and text controls, collaborative layers, and an Excalidraw-like experience; one participant explicitly frames the improvement as worth paying for. This is a demand signal, not observed conversion.
rows.title: Foundry users report a recurring desire for better drawing and whiteboard tools

rows.statement: Native Foundry drawings plus Precise Drawing Tools, Alternative Drawing Tools, Better Text Drawings, Wayfinder Wall Control, Dungeon Draw, Owlbear, and Miro cover much of the obvious freehand, text, wall, collaboration, and export surface.
rows.title: Generic Foundry drawing is already a populated category

rows.statement: MapForge is listed for current Foundry v14 and combines asset libraries, floors, textures, paths, walls, doors, windows, lighting, atmosphere, prefabs, animation, and flatten/export workflows. It materially closes the paid â€œbetter visual map authoringâ€ gap.
rows.title: MapForge is a current paid Foundry map-studio competitor

rows.statement: The demand is credible, but a new module would need to displace native tools, several active modules, Owlbear, Miro, and MapForge. A map-to-playable-geometry or package-completeness audit is a narrower creator feature, not the requested wide player market.
rows.title: Generic drawing and whiteboard should be rejected as a standalone product

rows.statement: Official 2024 rules define Study as an action for making Intelligence checks about memory, books, clues, and knowledge across Arcana, History, Investigation, Nature, and Religion. The rules do not themselves provide a persistent VTT knowledge workflow.
rows.title: The 2024 D&D Study action makes creature knowledge an ordinary play hook

rows.statement: Community discussions repeatedly address what a character should know about a creature, how to avoid player metagaming, and how to reveal useful lore without handing over a complete statblock. The incidence and payment value still require direct GM validation.
rows.title: Creature knowledge disputes create a recurring player and GM problem

rows.statement: ANewFoe hides unknown monsters, tracks known creatures per player, changes token presentation, reveals information after identification, and supports GM approval/DC modifiers. Its listing targets Foundry 12+ and shows older v12 verification/update evidence, so it is category proof rather than current v14 certification.
rows.title: ANewFoe proves the D&D5e concept but has an older support trail

rows.statement: PF2E Bestiary Tracking is a current Foundry v14 package with GM/player bestiary views and selective information reveal. It validates buyer value in one system while demonstrating that D&D5e and PF2e data/permissions need separate adapters.
rows.title: PF2E Bestiary Tracking validates selective bestiary reveal on current Foundry

rows.statement: The working promise is â€œYour character knows, even when you do notâ€: an unknown silhouette or alias becomes a player-safe field-guide entry after Study or evidence, rather than exposing a generic statblock or adding another permanent HUD.
rows.title: Monster Field Guide has a distinct player-facing promise

rows.statement: A useful record can separate identity/type/behavior, visible traits, resistances/weaknesses, and deeper lore, while recording evidence such as a check, observed regeneration, book research, GM approval, uncertainty, or rumor.
rows.title: Tiered reveal and provenance make the candidate more than a bestiary viewer

rows.statement: Mystery, horror, monster-hunt, and long-campaign GMs have clearer recurring value than a generic player audience; players are the users and beneficiaries, but the GM controls module purchase and campaign policy.
rows.title: The likely payer is a GM with repeated knowledge-heavy play

rows.statement: The checked sources prove demand signals and category implementations but do not prove a D&D5e GM will pay. A live choice among $5, $10, $15, $20, and no purchase plus a scheduled pilot is required.
rows.title: No observed price evidence yet supports Monster Field Guide

rows.statement: The first version should read installed actor data and GM-entered or user-provided notes, and should not distribute copied Monster Manual text, protected art, or an unlicensed lore library. Tool behavior is safer than republishing protected content.
rows.title: The rights-safe product boundary is customer-owned data

rows.statement: A portable packet can represent creature identity, player, evidence event, reveal tier, provenance, uncertainty, and capability requirements. Live actor reads, permissions, rolls, cards, and chat require separate Foundry, PF2e, Roll20, or other adapters.
rows.title: Cross-VTT portability belongs at the neutral knowledge-packet layer

rows.statement: The target fixture should use synthetic actors and two users to test unknown-state projection, Study or equivalent check, GM approval, tiered reveal, per-player persistence, reconnect, duplicate suppression, permission denial, and authoritative read-back on Foundry 14.367 / D&D5e 5.3.3.
rows.title: Monster Field Guide needs a smaller exact disposable fixture

rows.statement: Show an unknown creature becoming a tiered, player-safe field-guide entry in 20â€“30 seconds, then compare the GM's actual workaround and ask for a one-time price and scheduled pilot. Player enthusiasm or survey-only interest is not payment evidence.
rows.title: A silent visual demo and real price choice are the correct next market gate

rows.statement: Advance only if qualified GMs recognize a recent incident, prefer the workflow over the real workaround, choose non-zero payment, schedule pilots, and the fixture protects hidden knowledge. Otherwise reject the candidate and reopen the fresh product search.
rows.title: Monster Field Guide is a conditional lead, not an approved product

rows.statement: A current Foundry wish-list discussion asks for a focused drag-offer/accept trade window and small chat receipt, which is a recurring usability complaint but not direct payment evidence.
rows.title: Players request simple item and currency exchange

rows.statement: Item Piles supports robust player trading, merchants, and loot; Give Items Between Players, Let's Trade 5e, Shop, and RPGX Loot Crate cover focused, system-specific, or paid/free-tier variants.
rows.title: Current Foundry trading substitutes already cover the obvious logistics job

rows.statement: Foundry journals/map notes, Campaign Codex, World & Campaign Builder, external LegendKeeper/Obsidian workflows, and Familiar already address linked lore, shared notes, search, and memory.
rows.title: Campaign knowledge and player-facing notes are recurring but crowded

rows.statement: These jobs recur, but their alternatives are mature, familiar, free, subscription-backed, or already paid. A new product would need a sharply differentiated outcome rather than another organizer or transfer dialog.
rows.title: Generic trade, treasury, campaign wiki, and AI memory should not be fresh wide-market products

rows.statement: The current ANewFoe listing explicitly includes hidden unknown monsters, per-player known state, token-picture switching, basic-stat reveal, bulk upload, GM approval, and DC modifiers.
rows.title: ANewFoe covers nearly the full baseline Monster Field Guide workflow

rows.statement: ANewFoe lists available release 1.0.3 as Foundry 12+ / Verified 12 with an old update trail, while the official D&D5e system has an actively maintained 6.0.x line. This supports a compatibility hypothesis only; it does not show that customers will migrate.
rows.title: ANewFoe leaves a possible modern-target maintenance gap but not a proven market gap

rows.statement: PF2E Bestiary Tracking is current on Foundry v14 and provides GM/player bestiary views with selective reveal, validating the category while showing that system adapters and data boundaries are real work.
rows.title: PF2E Bestiary Tracking demonstrates current selective-reveal value in another system

rows.statement: A candidate must connect Study or observed events to GM-approved tiered facts, per-player provenance, uncertainty, persistent codex entries, and an immediate player-facing visual change. A generic bestiary or statblock viewer is already occupied.
rows.title: The remaining Monster Field Guide wedge is evidence-to-knowledge, not bestiary storage

rows.statement: Keep it as the research lead only until a side-by-side ANewFoe/manual/Study comparison produces a real GM price choice and scheduled pilot. If modernization is its only advantage, reject it and reopen the search.
rows.title: Monster Field Guide confidence was downgraded after direct competition re-audit

rows.statement: The package-only dbx-test-world fixture passed explicit data-path, world, process, port, version, and HTTP-readiness checks for Foundry 14.367 / D&D5e 5.3.3.
rows.title: The exact disposable Foundry target starts and reaches the native setup/join surface

rows.statement: The fixture join page had zero users and free-text credentials; the native setup/admin surface was reachable, but creating the synthetic GM/Player3 accounts was a separate native user-management operation and was not bypassed.
rows.title: Per-user hidden-state behavior remains blocked by missing synthetic users

rows.statement: The probe used only the isolated fixture, recorded zero world-document writes and no Ballad access, dismissed the optional usage-data prompt without enabling sharing, and stopped with no listener on port 30002.
rows.title: The exact runtime probe preserved the campaign-data boundary

rows.statement: Startup and setup UI are proven, but per-user projection, GM approval, Study/equivalent action, persistence, reconnect, duplicate suppression, and hidden-state protection remain untested.
rows.title: Monster Field Guide exact runtime evidence is partial, not a readiness claim

rows.statement: Current community requests and defect reports describe duplicate actors/assets, empty or unconfigured documents, broken UUID/file paths, orphaned token references, and invalid data that can surface after migration or package changes. This establishes recurring operational pain but not payment.
rows.title: Foundry users repeatedly need world cleanup and preflight diagnosis

rows.statement: Foundry provides backup, package compatibility, and migration guidance; Sephral's Content Backup & Restore handles named document recovery; Lore Reference Board repairs links in its own import/export surface; fvtt-world-tools handles file-oriented cleanup; Dedupe This! is stale. No checked source establishes a current whole-world diagnosis-and-repair product.
rows.title: Foundry and current tools cover pieces of world safety but not one evidence-linked preflight

rows.statement: A differentiated product would scan a world and its dependencies, show the affected object and evidence path, preview a narrow repair, snapshot before writing, reread the authoritative result, and produce an undo receipt. A backup, red/amber/green compatibility badge, or duplicate finder alone is insufficient.
rows.title: The World Doctor wedge is diagnosis plus reversible repair, not backup or deduplication

rows.statement: The buyer controls the world, module stack, backups, and upgrade decision; players benefit indirectly from fewer broken sessions. The strongest cohort is a GM with a long-running/import-heavy world or a recent upgrade/data incident, not an arbitrary player.
rows.title: The likely payer for World Doctor is the GM or host with expensive campaign state

rows.statement: The front door should show â€œIs my world safe to update tonight?â€ with an evidence-linked defect, repair preview, and verified result. â€œDatabase cleanupâ€ or â€œcompatibility dashboardâ€ would make the value invisible or interchangeable.
rows.title: The eye-catching World Doctor promise is safe-to-update confidence

rows.statement: A portable report can represent document references, asset paths, dependency edges, severity, confidence, suggested repair, and recovery receipts. Foundry document APIs, backups, permissions, and migration behavior require a separate adapter for every other VTT.
rows.title: World Doctor can share a neutral health report but not a universal live repair engine

rows.statement: Advance only if qualified GMs with recent incidents prefer the evidence-linked diagnosis and reversible repair, choose a non-zero price, schedule a pilot, and the exact fixture proves no false green, hidden write, or unrecoverable repair. Otherwise reopen the search.
rows.title: World Doctor is a conditional fresh candidate, not a selected product

rows.statement: Community reports describe system or module updates breaking sheets, modules, or campaign behavior; users respond with archived worlds, backups, manual repair, or stopping updates mid-campaign. This supports recurring pain but does not establish current market size or payment.
rows.title: Foundry upgrade incidents create real but directional GM cost

rows.statement: Foundry provides built-in backups, package backups, snapshots, and rollback, while hosting/support guidance directs users toward compatibility diagnosis, disabling modules, downgrading, and restoring an export. A backup manager is therefore not a fresh product wedge.
rows.title: Backup and support already cover the obvious recovery job

rows.statement: A potential product gap remains between a package snapshot and a healthy playable world: evidence-linked diagnosis of asset paths, behavioral/module interactions, malformed shapes, and orphaned references, followed by a previewed, narrow, verifiable, reversible repair.
rows.title: The remaining wedge is preflight diagnosis plus reversible repair

rows.statement: A current community pricing discussion reports fatigue with roughly $7â€“10/month creator subscriptions and preference for buy-once or flat support, while also showing that Foundry users do pay for modules/content. This is directional category evidence, not World Doctor willingness to pay.
rows.title: Directional pricing evidence favors buy-once or flat support testing

rows.statement: Use $15, $25, and $39 as initial buyer-choice anchors for a one-time GM/host utility. These are research design choices; a price is evidence only when a qualified buyer chooses it and accepts a disposable-copy pilot.
rows.title: Initial World Doctor price anchors are $15, $25, and $39 one-time

rows.statement: Keep the candidate only if qualified GMs prefer evidence-linked preflight and reversible repair over their real workaround, choose a non-zero price, and complete a safe fixture/pilot. Reject a prettier backup, generic compatibility dashboard, duplicate finder, or warning list that leaves diagnosis to the buyer.
rows.title: World Doctor remains conditional and must not become a backup manager

rows.statement: Community requests describe a repeated cost: the GM is willing to configure audio before play but does not want to change music manually during combat, and wants phase, actor, boss, turn, and end-of-combat transitions. This is directional user evidence, not payment proof.
rows.title: GMs want combat audio to run without interrupting narration

rows.statement: Minstrel, Combat Music Master, Dynamic Soundscapes, Soundscape Adventure, and Playlist Plus cover overlapping console, mixer, mood, soundscape, scene, combat, turn, region, priority, and transition features. Any new product must win beyond â€œplay and organize audio.â€
rows.title: Current Foundry audio tools cover consoles, moods, cues, and basic combat triggers

rows.statement: A candidate wedge is an event-to-condition-to-transition-to-action graph covering combat phase, round, actor/turn, HP threshold, scene/region, weights, cooldown, safe crossfade/ducking, correction, and emergency stop. Public descriptions show pieces but do not establish the full combination in one current tool.
rows.title: The possible gap is a declarative encounter event graph

rows.statement: A short clip can show exploration changing to combat, a pre-combat sting, boss escalation, low-health transition, and victory without GM clicks. This is more eye-catching and repeatable than an invisible maintenance report, but presentation does not prove purchase.
rows.title: Battle Director has an immediately visible demo promise

rows.statement: Current Foundry audio modules and sound libraries use publisher purchases, Patreon access, or lifetime options, while users report subscription fatigue. Test a one-time utility at $15, $25, and $39 without bundling copyrighted music.
rows.title: Audio automation has category-level paid precedent but no direct WTP proof

rows.statement: A neutral recipe can encode event, condition, transition, action, asset reference, weight, cooldown, and recovery state. Foundry combat/actor/HP hooks and other VTT APIs still require separate system adapters.
rows.title: An event graph can be portable while live events remain adapter-specific

rows.statement: Advance only if qualified GMs prefer no-touch event-graph audio over their current workflow and current point tools, choose a non-zero one-time price, complete a pilot, and the fixture proves correct bounded transitions with a reliable stop. Otherwise reopen the search.
rows.title: Battle Director is a challenger, not a selected product

rows.statement: Foundry v14 documents combat start/turn hooks, generic Actor/document update hooks, Playlist play/stop/next operations, and Sound play/fade/stop controls. This establishes a plausible API surface, not exact runtime certification.
rows.title: Foundry exposes the core Battle Director signal and playback primitives

rows.statement: The D&D5e system documents current HP at system.attributes.hp.value and exposes system-specific hooks/data that can be observed by a Foundry module. System adapters remain necessary for other games.
rows.title: D&D5e exposes a usable HP threshold path

rows.statement: The local Boss Engine fixture observes updateActor, updateCombat, and D&D5e activity/roll hooks while using active-GM gating, a mutation queue, sync guard, debounce, and multi-phase HP/state transitions. This proves reusable local patterns, not Battle Director audio certification.
rows.title: The local disposable fixture contains reusable event/state feasibility evidence

rows.statement: combatStart is initiating-client/pre-update while combatTurnChange is all-clients/post-update. A safe product must elect an active GM, fingerprint events, suppress duplicate delivery, and synchronize one committed audio state rather than letting every client react independently.
rows.title: Foundry hook timing requires one transition authority

rows.statement: Playlist and Sound APIs expose playback and fading, but the current local evidence does not prove synchronized cross-client audio, browser autoplay behavior, reconnect resynchronization, or stop guarantees in the exact Foundry 14.367 / D&D5e 5.3.3 fixture.
rows.title: The exact two-client audio path remains unproven

rows.statement: Roll20 provides Pro Mod Script event handlers for turn order, graphics, and attributes plus Jukebox controls; Owlbear provides an extension SDK/broadcast surface but no shared D&D combat/HP contract. A neutral event graph is portable, live event/playback mappings are not universal.
rows.title: Cross-VTT support is feasible only through separate adapters

rows.statement: Do not bundle, scrape, or redistribute music. Reference customer-owned/local audio or VTT asset IDs through adapters; treat a future audio catalog as a separate rights and service business.
rows.title: Customer-owned audio keeps the first product rights boundary manageable

rows.statement: Video Game Music covers area and combat music, token themes, priority, fallback modes, crossfade, playback-position memory, and suppression.
rows.title: Video Game Music closes much of the playback-control gap

rows.statement: An abandoned adaptive-audio module and user requests for HP-reactive music indicate maintenance pain or interest, but they do not establish willingness to pay or prove that a new product owns an unmet buyer problem.
rows.title: Adaptive Audio abandonment is maintenance evidence only

rows.statement: A system-neutral graph editor combining triggers, weights, cooldowns, previews, portable recipes, and recovery may still be useful, but it looks like a power-user authoring tool and is not yet evidence of broad ordinary-player demand.
rows.title: The remaining audio graph gap is narrow and unproven

rows.statement: Direct competitors close the original adaptive-audio wedge. Continue only if qualified GMs name a repeated unmet cost after comparing current modules and choose a non-zero price plus a pilot.
rows.title: Demote Battle Director and reopen the fresh search

rows.statement: Recent community requests describe Active Tile Triggers as valuable but ask for a simpler workflow. The recurring payer problem is not missing trigger capability; it is configuring reliable doors, traps, teleports, reveals, prompts, sound, and effects without learning a dependency stack.
rows.title: GMs want interactive scenes without macro-stack setup

rows.statement: Monk's Active Tile Triggers supports teleportation, doors, visibility, sound, notifications, chat, macros, roll tables, effects, movement, and fog reset; Foundry Scene Regions provide native event/behavior primitives. A new product must win on composition, testing, recovery, and discoverability.
rows.title: Raw scene interaction capability already exists

rows.statement: A short demo can show a player entering a region, triggering a trap roll, opening a door, revealing a hidden area, and receiving a prompt or effect. The visual cause-and-effect is easier to market than invisible maintenance work.
rows.title: Scene Interaction Studio has a visible demo payoff

rows.statement: Community posts describe slow map and asset setup, while MapForge, Moulinette, quick import, Dungeon Alchemist, and Dungeondraft occupy the current buyer workflow. No new map product is selected from this scan.
rows.title: Quick map building is a real pain but crowded

rows.statement: Swipe, Diecast, VTT Companion, and Sheet Only address mobile player workflows; Smart Combat NPC and Automated NPCs address D&D5e NPC automation. These are valid market signals but not clean new wedges without a distinct buyer promise.
rows.title: Mobile companions and NPC autopilot are already active paid categories

rows.statement: Advance only if ordinary GMs prefer guided scene interaction over their real Active Tile/Region workflow, choose a non-zero one-time price, complete a pilot, and can reuse a neutral recipe without hidden macros or unresolved UUIDs.
rows.title: Scene Interaction Studio is a provisional fresh challenger

rows.statement: Glyph for Foundry v14 provides a visual program editor, branches, loops, delays, expanded events, token/tile/audio/chat actions, dialogs/journals, system-aware rolls, and MATT import. This materially overlaps the proposed Scene Interaction Studio promise.
rows.title: Glyph closes the visual scene-automation wedge

rows.statement: Foundry Scene Regions support shapes, enter/exit/move events, teleportation, behavior toggles, scrolling text, macro/script hooks, and active effects. A new product must solve a buyer failure beyond exposing these primitives.
rows.title: Foundry Regions already provide a native interaction base

rows.statement: Because Glyph, MATT, and native Regions cover the proposed no-macro scene interaction promise, do not implement the candidate unless a buyer names a remaining repeated failure and chooses a non-zero price plus pilot. Continue the fresh search outside visual scene automation.
rows.title: Scene Interaction Studio is demoted

rows.statement: Community reports describe players waiting minutes for scene assets, periodic freezes despite low latency, and the need for explicit knowledge of when all clients finished preloading. This is directional repeated-incident evidence, not payment proof.
rows.title: Mixed-client scene loading can consume live session time
