rows.statement: Preload Tracker covers scene/audio preloading and markers; Performance Optimizer covers profiles, GM controls, low-FPS suggestions, and benchmarks; Axon's Performance Monitor covers diagnostics and reports. None of these descriptions alone establishes an end-to-end quorum gate with fallback and activation receipt.
rows.title: Current readiness solutions are fragmented

rows.statement: A red/amber/green readiness board can show which client is ready, which is slow, what fallback is selected, and when the next scene is safe to activate. This makes a reliability product visible without bundling content.
rows.title: Session Ready has a visible reliability demo

rows.statement: The candidate combines scene/audio preflight, per-player readiness, quorum policy, low-quality fallback, stale-client detection, manual override, and a redacted receipt. This is a workflow gap hypothesis, not proof that current modules cannot be composed to do it.
rows.title: The possible product is an end-to-end readiness protocol

rows.statement: A neutral protocol can encode readiness state, quorum, asset budget, fallback policy, and receipt. Foundry preload, browser metrics, scene activation, and quality controls require a native adapter; other VTTs need separate observation.
rows.title: Readiness state is portable but client controls are adapter-specific

rows.statement: Advance only if qualified remote or hybrid GMs prefer the end-to-end gate over current point tools, choose a non-zero one-time price, and complete a mixed-client pilot without false-ready or stuck-session behavior.
rows.title: Session Ready is a provisional challenger

rows.statement: Preload Tracker 2.2.0 reports per-user asset load times, includes scene audio in the preload log, enables Activate when every connected user reaches 100%, marks a client stuck at 100% with an orange check, and can skip scene audio during preload. The core readiness/quorum promise is therefore already implemented by a current point module.
rows.title: Preload Tracker now closes the Session Ready activation gate

rows.statement: Performance Optimizer provides per-player performance profiles, GM remote controls, low-FPS detection/suggestions, and live client charts. Axon's Performance Monitor provides group views, client status, reports, network/canvas loading diagnostics, and a crash flight recorder. A new readiness product must identify a failure beyond this combination.
rows.title: Performance and group diagnostics already cover the remaining Session Ready surface

rows.statement: Combining existing preload and monitoring modules would be a convenience bundle rather than a new payer problem. Session-loading pain remains a recruiting signal, but implementation is rejected unless buyers name a repeated unmet failure and choose a non-zero price plus pilot.
rows.title: Session Ready is demoted after direct source audit

rows.statement: A recent high-engagement Foundry request asks for a Last Known Position ghost so players can remember where enemies were seen after leaving line of sight. The signal is stronger than a generic feature wish but still directional and not payment proof.
rows.title: Last-seen enemy memory has direct player-facing demand

rows.statement: Foundry core fog preserves explored map memory but not individual hostile-token last positions. Shared Token Visibility shares currently revealed tokens; Roll20 Explorer Mode preserves explored map areas; Owlbear Smoke & Spectre provides per-token visibility. The source scan did not identify a current v14 package that combines observer-scoped, decaying hostile-token last-seen ghosts, but private macros or unpublished work may exist.
rows.title: Current visibility tools do not publish the full Tactical Memory workflow

rows.statement: A translucent enemy silhouette fading behind a wall communicates the benefit in seconds and supports stealth, pursuit, dungeon, ambush, and split-party encounters without requiring content creation or AI.
rows.title: Tactical Memory has an eye-catching ordinary-play demo

rows.statement: The portable contract is observer scope, token binding, observed position, round/time, uncertainty, and expiry. Foundry needs canvas/visibility adapters; Roll20 needs an API script; Owlbear Rodeo needs an extension. Cross-VTT parity remains unverified.
rows.title: Tactical Memory can use a neutral observation ledger

rows.statement: Advance only if qualified GMs prefer last-seen ghosts over core fog, current visibility modules, or manual markers, choose a non-zero one-time price, and complete a disposable stealth encounter without information leakage.
rows.title: Tactical Memory is a provisional fresh challenger

rows.statement: Battle Replay uses temporary ghost tokens for after-the-fact playback; Group Tokens and Foundry movement history describe controlled token movement; Movement Approval shows prospective player paths; Shared Token Visibility shares currently revealed tokens. These are adjacent substitutes, not the full observer-scoped, decaying live hostile-token memory workflow.
rows.title: Adjacent ghost and movement tools do not close live Tactical Memory

rows.statement: The hard runtime problem is capturing the exact last permitted view for each observer without leaking a hidden token's current position, then converging after movement, visibility changes, reconnect, expiry, and GM correction. API existence and a visual ghost do not certify this behavior.
rows.title: Tactical Memory has a per-player observation correctness risk

rows.statement: The first slice must be temporary, player-safe, and focused on dungeon/combat use. It must not become a fog-of-war replacement, replay engine, or campaign-history database before buyer and runtime gates pass.
rows.title: Tactical Memory is narrowed to a live encounter overlay

rows.statement: Player Perspective is a current paid v13-v14 publisher module for simulating each player's fog, token visibility, and restricted assets. Stage Master is a current paid v14 product offering shared vision, fog tools, party views, camera control, and player-facing direction. This supports category-level willingness to pay but is not product-specific WTP for last-seen ghosts.
rows.title: Paid visibility and table-control products establish category precedent

rows.statement: Foundry v14 documents the sightRefresh hook, CanvasVisibility.testVisibility, token vision/visibility data, and canvas visibility refresh methods. A player-local observer can potentially record only a token that is currently visible, then render a temporary marker after it leaves view; this remains static feasibility, not runtime certification.
rows.title: Foundry v14 exposes a plausible local observation boundary

rows.statement: A player client may technically enumerate token documents, but memory must only be created after the current client confirms observation. The default should be private local memory; party mode may transmit only an already-observed historical record and never a GM's current hidden position or actor data.
rows.title: Tactical Memory must never derive or broadcast raw hidden token positions

rows.statement: Premium-module existence and community statements about paid tools are category proxies only. The candidate must pass a direct $5/$10/$15/no-purchase choice and disposable pilot before any price, marketability, or implementation claim is accepted.
rows.title: Tactical Memory has no established price yet

rows.statement: A recent request thread contains demands for zero-prep modules, mobile access, persistent spreadsheet-like scene state, journal/window organization, Bastion expansion, and Last Known Position. These establish candidate recruiting signals, not a willingness-to-pay ranking.
rows.title: The broad community scan contains several payer problems but weak ranking evidence

rows.statement: Stage Master and Player Perspective cover player-view/session presentation; SessionFlow and Whiteboard Experience cover shared canvases/state; mobile companion products cover device access; v14 core popouts address window organization; and Indy Ventures covers much of the Bastion/enterprise loop. Candidate selection must therefore use direct gaps, not broad feature popularity.
rows.title: Most broader candidates have current substitutes

rows.statement: Tactical Memory combines direct player-facing demand, high demo clarity, a possible neutral observation ledger, and fewer identified exact competitors, but its buyer breadth is medium, its privacy/runtime risk is high, and its product-specific WTP is unproven.
rows.title: Tactical Memory leads the shortlist but does not meet the wide-market bar yet

rows.statement: The buyer test must show paid visibility tools, shared-state tools, a mobile option, current Bastion tools, and a zero-prep/general-state alternative so Tactical Memory is selected only if it changes a real workflow rather than merely producing the best demo.
rows.title: A visual feature must not win by omission of controls

rows.statement: Community reports describe unexpected locations and the need to produce a usable map or visual board while running the session, sometimes in seconds rather than 20â€“30 minutes. This is a real recruiting signal but not product-specific payment evidence.
rows.title: Improvised encounters create repeated preparation pressure

rows.statement: Dungeon Draw v14 supports live room/wall/door/theme drawing, procedural generation, undo/redo, and scene/lighting updates; Quickdraw provides temporary live drawings; SessionFlow provides a tactical map workspace and quick scenes. Quick Encounters is stale after v12 but its packaging concept does not create a clean new wedge alone.
rows.title: Current tools already cover most zero-prep encounter-board primitives

rows.statement: A temporary no-world-mutation encounter board could be useful, but it is close to Dungeon Draw plus Quickdraw and current scene tools. Reopen only if a buyer identifies a repeated failure around cleanup, token placement, or safe ephemeral state and pays for a pilot.
rows.title: Instant Encounter Board is demoted as a separate product

rows.statement: Foundry module and licensing guidance permits functionality modules and paid publication subject to rights. A first Tactical Memory slice can ship original code with a procedural/local ghost or silhouette, no bundled art, music, token catalog, publisher text, or cloud service, and an explicit manifest license. Avoid WotC/D&D assets and copied rules text.
rows.title: Tactical Memory can avoid third-party content liability in its first slice

rows.statement: A neutral record can contain observer scope, VTT/scene binding, observed token binding, observed position/elevation, round/time, uncertainty, and expiry/correction. Foundry is the first adapter; Roll20 would require its Pro Mod Script/API surface and Owlbear would require its extension/storage/broadcast model. A shared ledger does not prove runtime parity.
rows.title: Cross-VTT portability is a neutral observation protocol plus separate adapters

rows.statement: Original/local presentation makes rights risk low and manageable, but buyer breadth, product-specific willingness to pay, privacy correctness, and exact runtime behavior remain unproven. The fresh search must continue instead of treating portability or clean licensing as demand.
rows.title: Rights cleanliness removes an objection but does not validate the product

rows.statement: Community discussion asks for per-player language handling, and current gaming-tool projects are emerging around live translation for international groups. This is a recruiting signal for bilingual families, international friends, and online communities, not direct willingness-to-pay proof.
rows.title: Mixed-language tables are a recurring player-facing candidate problem

rows.statement: Polyglot handles fictional-language obfuscation and character language knowledge; Comprehend Languages and Journal Translator focus on journals, item text, or selected text; Small World is the closest instant chat translation precedent but is listed for Foundry v9-10. The gap is plausible in current Foundry, not greenfield.
rows.title: Current translation tools solve adjacent rather than live per-user table translation

rows.statement: A Foundry-first typed-chat translation layer with per-user language choice, source preservation, and optional captions has an immediately understandable demo and player-facing benefit. Buyer breadth, translation trust, provider cost, privacy, and cross-VTT demand remain unproven.
rows.title: TableSpeak is a fresh multilingual-table challenger

rows.statement: Small World proves prior Foundry demand/attempt; Cibola 8 advertises broad translation but not the same low-latency per-user chat workflow; external Discord and desktop translators can be good enough because voice commonly happens outside the VTT. The product must prove a VTT-specific advantage rather than claim no alternatives.
rows.title: TableSpeak must be positioned against external translation workarounds

rows.statement: Voice adds speaker attribution, audio capture and consent, latency, provider cost, terminology errors, and failure recovery. Typed chat plus optional caption output can use Foundry's chat hook and caption surface with a clearer fallback boundary.
rows.title: Live voice translation is too risky for the first TableSpeak claim

rows.statement: Do not market to anyone who merely wants a translated interface. Recruit organizers of mixed-language tables, compare external workarounds, and ask for a $5/$10/$15 one-time BYOK/local purchase plus a three-session pilot.
rows.title: The TableSpeak payer is a table organizer with a repeated language failure

rows.statement: Google Cloud Translation publishes a free monthly character allowance followed by usage pricing, while DeepL exposes developer APIs and separate paid API/voice plans. A one-time module cannot promise unlimited hosted usage without caps or a local model.
rows.title: Translation providers make BYOK plausible but hosted usage is metered

rows.statement: Foundry v14 documents the chatMessage hook for messages sent through ChatLog, and libCaptions provides a display surface for caption-producing modules. This supports an M0 typed-chat proof but not provider quality, privacy, or cross-VTT certification.
rows.title: Foundry provides a narrow typed-chat integration surface

rows.statement: A one-time module can delegate provider choice and usage to the table owner or run a capped local path. A hosted plan would add subscription/credit pricing, data handling, outage recovery, and abuse controls. The buyer test must not conflate these offers.
rows.title: TableSpeak must separate one-time BYOK/local and hosted offers

rows.statement: Discord's App Directory includes translation apps; BabelBot advertises per-user text translation and paid image/live-voice features, while TradLinker and desktop tools target international gaming communities. TableSpeak cannot claim general translation demand as an unserved market.
rows.title: External translation apps already cover general multilingual communication

rows.statement: A VTT-specific translator could preserve roll cards, document links, whispers, speaker/token identity, and private per-user rendering without duplicating every translation in shared chat. This advantage is a hypothesis that must beat Discord/desktop substitutes in a real table.
rows.title: TableSpeak's only defensible wedge is VTT-semantic preservation

rows.statement: The buyer segment narrows to mixed-language Foundry tables that already tried external translation and still lose VTT context. Keep a price/pilot gate open, but reopen the fresh search instead of treating the international-gamer category as sufficient.
rows.title: TableSpeak is conditional rather than broadly marketable today

rows.statement: Community questions describe difficulty finding level-up controls and players using external builders for progression. This is a valid recruiting signal for new and returning players, but not product-specific payment evidence.
rows.title: Guided character progression is a recurring player onboarding problem

rows.statement: D&D5e Character Builder provides guided creation, level-up, multiclass, validation, and tutorials; Hero Mancer also covers D&D5e creation/level-up; PF2e Level-Up Wizard and PF2e Leveler cover guided Pathfinder progression. A generic Level-Up Concierge would duplicate current products.
rows.title: Current v14 progression packages occupy the guided level-up gap

rows.statement: A cross-system explanation layer might still help players, but the product would enter the crowded HUD/player-cockpit space and inherit system-specific rules maintenance. No clean new payer gap is established.
rows.title: Level-Up Concierge is demoted as a separate product

rows.statement: Community workflows describe players wanting access to images, letters, maps, and other handouts after a one-time Show Players reveal. Native ownership and journal-folder workarounds can solve it, but the repeated request is evidence of a workflow problem rather than payment.
rows.title: Players repeatedly need previously shown visual artifacts

rows.statement: Nik's Show & Tell improves image sharing and chat integration; Handout Ping Viewer adds synchronized viewing and pings; Investigation Board turns images and linked objects into a collaborative evidence board. Their public descriptions do not establish automatic per-player history for every authorized reveal, but absence is not proof of demand.
rows.title: Foundry presentation modules cover sharing but not proven automatic receipt history

rows.statement: A Foundry-first gallery that records only already-authorized reveals and reopens the original permitted document or link has a clear player-visible demo. It remains unselected until it beats native journals and manual ownership at a non-zero price.
rows.title: Evidence Locker is a fresh conditional challenger

rows.statement: LoreBox advertises real-time handout delivery, organized campaign assets, and a personal collection across past sessions; TableWeaver offers a GM-controlled player display; Roll20 and Owlbear provide native or extension-based handout surfaces. Broad handout delivery is therefore not an open category.
rows.title: External products already sell handout delivery and recall

rows.statement: The candidate must capture authorized reveals without a second service, preserve per-player permissions and revocation, reopen current linked Foundry documents or roll/item cards, and provide a session receipt. A generic gallery or handout app is already substituted.
rows.title: The only defensible Evidence Locker wedge is VTT-semantic automatic capture

rows.statement: A neutral receipt can carry artifact identity, recipients, session/time, caption, source reference, and revoke state, but Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear expose different document, storage, and permission APIs. A second-VTT adapter requires its own safety and reconnect proof.
rows.title: Artifact receipts do not prove cross-VTT parity

rows.statement: Community requests ask for system-agnostic torch timers and named world-clock reminders for wandering monsters, rituals, and resource expiration, including a narrative message at the boundary. This is a recruiting signal for exploration/survival tables, not willingness-to-pay proof.
rows.title: World-time resource automation is a concrete recurring request

rows.statement: A torch can be lit from inventory, count down as in-game time advances, and visibly expire with a player-facing cue. A neutral event record could support other VTTs, but buyer breadth is narrower than ordinary D&D play.
rows.title: World Clock Automator has an eye-catching consequence demo

rows.statement: The current v14 Light Sources module turns inventory items into light sources, consumes items, supports in-game or real-time duration, shows remaining time, and removes light on expiry. A new product cannot sell generic torch automation as an open category.
rows.title: Light Sources now closes the broad torch-timer gap

rows.statement: About Time exposes world-time events and reminders; Expedition Tracker provides expedition turns, timed effects, optional wandering-monster rolls, and light behavior; SessionFlow tracks travel, supply, fatigue, and progress clocks; Calendaria and Glyph provide conditional notes or world-time triggers.
rows.title: Existing world-time and effect tools cover much of the remainder

rows.statement: A possible gap is a visual authoring surface that binds world-time events to inventory, effects, chat visibility, and reversible consequences without macros or system-specific item assumptions. It must prove a repeated failure left by current tools.
rows.title: Only a no-code cross-system consequence workflow remains plausible

rows.statement: The request is real and the demo is clear, but current v14 packages cover the broad behavior and the likely payer segment is narrow. Keep event-record and consequence-preview mechanics as reusable assets, not a product selection.
rows.title: World Clock Automator is demoted as a standalone product

rows.statement: Recent community discussion describes large module stacks, long campaigns held back by migration risk, users stripping worlds down to avoid maintenance, and major updates causing uncertainty. This is a strong recruiting signal for qualified GMs, not a conversion rate.
rows.title: Foundry update and maintenance anxiety is a strong recurring GM pain signal

rows.statement: Foundry provides package backups, snapshots, restore, compatibility metadata, and migration guidance; Sephral's Content Backup & Restore handles named document recovery; Asset Auditor checks missing file paths; Find the Culprit isolates likely module conflicts; FileSmith verifies file/document operations; Scene Packer repairs links during packaging.
rows.title: Current tools cover backups, recovery, asset auditing, isolation, file operations, and packaging

rows.statement: The defensible gap is an evidence-linked answer to what will break after a specific update, backed by a disposable-copy smoke test, explicit risk report, previewed repair, authoritative reread, and recovery receipt. Warnings, snapshots, and backup lists alone are insufficient.
rows.title: World Doctor must be a pre-session rehearsal, not another backup browser

rows.statement: Casual one-shot users are a negative control because a backup or reinstall may be enough. The strongest payer hypothesis is a GM/host with a persistent or paid campaign, a substantial module stack, and a recent incident or near miss.
rows.title: The likely World Doctor payer is a long-running or paid module-heavy GM

rows.statement: Community pricing discussion favors buy-once or bounded support over accumulating creator subscriptions. Test $15, $25, and $39 against no purchase; these are anchors for a behavioral test, not observed willingness-to-pay.
rows.title: World Doctor requires a buy-once price test rather than subscription assumption

rows.statement: A neutral packet can contain package identity/version, asset fingerprints, check results, repair proposals, and recovery receipts. Foundry can be the first adapter; Roll20 and Owlbear require separate read-only probes because their live and storage APIs differ. Original code against user-owned worlds keeps licensing risk manageable.
rows.title: World Doctor has a portable diagnostic-packet boundary but not portable runtime parity

rows.statement: A recent high-engagement community request asks for better drawing tools, explicitly says the author would pay real money for an Excalidraw-like layer, and compares Foundry unfavorably with Roll20's drawing workflow. This is a strong recruiting and marketing signal, not observed conversion.
rows.title: Live map annotation has direct consumer-facing demand

rows.statement: The same scan surfaced simple player-to-player trade and mobile/tablet access requests, but Item Piles advertises robust trading while Swipe, PocketScroll, Sheet Only, and companion modules already address mobile or simplified player access. Neither is a clean new product gap.
rows.title: Player trade and mobile access are negative controls in the fresh scan

rows.statement: A fast, system-agnostic, touch/pen-friendly sketch layer could let a GM or permitted player draw, erase, label, measure, temporarily reveal, save, or discard annotations without leaving the active scene. The payer hypothesis is the live-play GM; player benefit is indirect.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook is the fresh drawing challenger

rows.statement: Foundry core provides freehand, shapes, polygons, text, and permission-controlled drawings. Precise Drawing Tools, Advanced Drawing Tools, Dungeon Draw, and Quickdraw cover precision, editing, mapping, and temporary annotations. A generic drawing overhaul would be a crowded category.
rows.title: Foundry core and current modules close generic drawing improvements

rows.statement: A defensible product would combine a floating touch/pen toolbar, private/party/GM-only layers, temporary marks with cleanup, saved snapshots, reversible layer promotion, journal/image annotation, and native export. The value is speed and scope safety, not more editor controls.
rows.title: The remaining Tactical Sketchbook wedge is a scoped live-play workflow

rows.statement: Gambit's Enhanced Drawing is being positioned as a premium early-access improvement, while current free modules and core features remain available. This shows that some users may pay for a better drawing workflow but does not establish a price for Tactical Sketchbook.
rows.title: Premium drawing competition is category precedent, not product WTP

rows.statement: The qualified payer is a GM who annotates or improvises during at least three sessions per month, runs theatre-of-the-mind/hexcrawl/investigation play, or uses a touchscreen, TV, or hybrid table. A GM who only imports finished battlemaps is a negative control.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook targets drawing-heavy live-play GMs

rows.statement: The storefront demo can show a blank or imported scene becoming a clear route, room, label, and player-facing annotation in under thirty seconds, then switch one mark to GM-only and discard or save it as a clean native layer. Test one-time $10/$20/$30 anchors against no purchase.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook has a short eye-catching product demonstration

rows.statement: A neutral vtt-sketch record can carry strokes/shapes/text, scope, scene or image anchor, style, author, revision, expiry, and export target. Foundry DrawingDocument, Roll20 drawing objects, and Owlbear extensions have different permissions, history, mobile, and performance boundaries, so the first proof must be Foundry-local.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook can port an annotation record, not identical editor behavior

rows.statement: Gambit's Image Viewer is a current v13+ / v14-verified premium module with GM-controlled real-time image/video annotations, pings, player editing, and optional saves. Gambit's Enhanced Drawing is positioned as a premium canvas drawing expansion with vector erasing, lasso selection, stamps, connectors, and shape recognition.
rows.title: Current Gambit products occupy the broad Tactical Sketchbook drawing category

rows.statement: Generic drawing improvement is no longer a clean gap. Only temporary route/area marks on the active map, scoped private/party/GM layers, automatic cleanup, and reversible promotion to native scene drawings remain distinct enough to test.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook is demoted to a narrow temporary scene-annotation hypothesis

rows.statement: A recent v14 discussion describes a GM spending about fifteen minutes searching journal entries during a session, making stored adventure content a concrete session-momentum pain signal. This is recruiting evidence, not conversion evidence.
rows.title: Adventure-running GMs report costly journal lookup during play

rows.statement: A local read-only lane could use the active scene, selected map note, opened adventure, or GM-selected location to surface relevant journal passages, linked actors/items/scenes, clues, maps, and next actions. The payer hypothesis is an adventure-running GM.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator is a fresh contextual-session challenger

rows.statement: Search and Highlight searches journal pages, actor names, and item names with text highlighting; Simple SearchBar and Quick Insert provide global keyboard search; Monk's Enhanced Journal adds description search, highlighting, bookmarks, tabs, and specialized sheets.
rows.title: Foundry v14 already has several maintained search and journal solutions

rows.statement: Campaign Codex provides relationships, tagging, permissions, quests, and tables of contents; World & Campaign Builder provides relationship-aware search and session planning as a free module; Simulacrum offers AI campaign document search and actions. A generic wiki, search bar, or copilot is not a clean gap.
rows.title: Campaign Codex, World & Campaign Builder, and AI tools cover broader organization

rows.statement: A defensible product would show ranked evidence with exact source links, a short dismissible â€œwhat can happen here?â€ runbook, and context from the current scene/location without rewriting content, using no cloud index or bundled adventure text.
rows.title: The remaining Adventure Navigator wedge is deterministic active-scene context

rows.statement: The qualified payer runs a purchased or imported adventure path, large campaign conversion, or journal-heavy homebrew at least monthly and recently lost time finding a passage, actor, map, clue, or procedure. Improvisation-only GMs are a negative control.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator targets GMs running imported or journal-heavy content

rows.statement: The storefront demo can select a scene or location and immediately show the exact boxed text, linked NPC, map, clue, and next action, then open the source document. Test $15/$25/$39 one-time anchors against no purchase.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator has a clear time-saved demonstration

rows.statement: A neutral record can contain source document ID, page/heading, scene/location anchor, relationship edges, evidence-excerpt hash, visibility scope, rank explanation, and dismissed/pinned state. Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear require separate content/handout adapters. Local hashes and source links reduce licensing risk.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator can port a context-index record without copying publisher content

rows.statement: JournalEntry exposes scene-note relationships, permission checks, user-specific visibility, and links to related documents; the journal model supports map pins and linked actors/items/scenes. This establishes static feasibility for a local index, not ranking, reconnect, or no-leak certification.
rows.title: Foundry v14 exposes a plausible read-only Adventure Navigator boundary

rows.statement: An index can become stale or contain records for GM-only pages. Results must be filtered against current user permission, source edits, deleted documents, and migrated IDs before display or source opening.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator must recheck permission at result and open time

rows.statement: The module should index user-owned worlds and installed content, keep excerpts as hashes or transient local data, and link to the authoritative document instead of shipping publisher text or art. This is a product boundary, not legal advice.
rows.title: A local hash and source-link design reduces but does not eliminate content rights risk

rows.statement: Source ID/page, scene or location anchor, relationship edges, excerpt hash, visibility scope, rank explanation, and pin/dismiss state can be represented neutrally. Roll20 handouts and Owlbear extensions require separate adapters for storage, permissions, search, and lifecycle.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator has a neutral context-index contract but no cross-VTT parity

rows.statement: Static API feasibility justifies a disposable Foundry fixture, but product selection still requires buyer choice, non-zero price, pilot, permission/stale-link correctness, and a second-VTT boundary.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator remains conditional after technical review

rows.statement: Community pain, package capabilities, and eye-catching demos are directional evidence only; none yet has three non-zero price choices or committed three-session pilots.
rows.title: No current candidate has product-specific willingness-to-pay or a scheduled pilot

rows.statement: It has an explicit recent lookup incident and a low-mutation, local-index boundary, but faces strong maintained search and campaign-organization competition.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator is the next empirical pilot candidate

rows.statement: It targets a higher-value long-running/module-heavy GM pain, but has a narrower payer segment and higher runtime/false-green risk than Adventure Navigator.
rows.title: World Doctor is the second empirical arm

rows.statement: Generic drawing demand is not enough to reopen the category; only a buyer-reported unresolved temporary live-scene workflow should reactivate it.
rows.title: Tactical Sketchbook is fallback-only after the current Gambit correction

rows.statement: A recent feature discussion describes missing Roll20's fast encounter-map workflow, layer/object-type friction, and the lack of an integrated image search. This is a recruiting signal, not conversion proof.
rows.title: Improvisation-heavy GMs report that rapid scene creation takes too many clicks

rows.statement: A Foundry-first lane could turn a background or blank grid into a playable temporary encounter board with user-owned assets, limited walls/lights/labels/tokens, and explicit player-safe promotion.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board is a fresh live-play staging challenger

rows.statement: The likely payer makes at least one unplanned encounter scene per session, runs hexcrawls or investigations, or regularly converts reference images during play. Map-making hobbyists and finished-map importers are negative controls.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board targets improvisation-heavy GMs

rows.statement: The marketing proof is a blank or reference image becoming a grid-aligned scene with a few assets, a token, and safe player reveal in thirty seconds. Test $15/$25/$39 against no purchase and a three-session pilot.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board has a visible timed demo

rows.statement: MapForge, FA Nexus, Moulinette, Scene Express, Mass Import, Forgotten Adventures assets, and external map makers cover broad scene creation, asset search, import, and map-authoring workflows.
rows.title: Generic rapid map-making is already crowded

rows.statement: A defensible product must be faster than a full editor, use only a small set of play-time controls, isolate private/party/GM layers, and promote a selected board to native scene data. Another map editor or asset browser should be rejected.
rows.title: The remaining Rapid Encounter Board wedge is temporary live encounter staging

rows.statement: A neutral package can carry a background reference, grid, token references, wall/light segments, labels, scope, temporary expiry, and promotion state. Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear need separate scene/object/storage adapters.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board has a neutral package boundary but no VTT parity

rows.statement: The candidate advances only if improvisation-heavy GMs choose it over MapForge, FA Nexus, Moulinette, and current import workflows at a non-zero price and complete a three-session pilot.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board remains conditional after direct competition

rows.statement: MapForge is presented as a commercial Foundry module with Patreon access, a visible development feedback loop, and buyer comments describing sign-up and strong early value. This validates a payer segment, not a new product.
rows.title: MapForge provides real category payment and adoption evidence

rows.statement: A commenter reports joining the lowest tier after seeing the demo, while other comments ask about subscription access, try-before-buy, performance, and asset-pack behavior. No conversion count or independent price distribution is observed.
rows.title: MapForge buyer comments are directional conversion evidence only

rows.statement: MapForge already demonstrates a full battlemap studio inside Foundry, including floors, walls, paths, objects, mood, lights/shadows, prefabs, flattening, and export. A new product cannot sell that same promise.
rows.title: MapForge owns the generic in-Foundry map-studio message

rows.statement: The only remaining marketability hypothesis is faster temporary live staging, lower asset/performance overhead, simpler player-safe promotion, or a credible one-time/no-subscription offer. Subscription fatigue alone is not a gap.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board must beat MapForge on a distinct workflow

rows.statement: Community reports include too many tabs, confusing sheets, and players struggling with Foundry, while other groups report that players adapt quickly once the GM limits the interface. This supports recruiting table owners but is not conversion evidence.
rows.title: Player complexity is a real but mixed consumer pain signal

rows.statement: A GM-authored session mode could guide join/claim, current-scene context, a small set of permitted actions, the next roll or decision, ready state, and fallback to the normal sheet. It is not a generic mobile sheet, UI skin, hero gallery, or character builder.
rows.title: TableStart is a fresh guided-player-session challenger

rows.statement: The strongest payer hypothesis is a GM who repeatedly onboards new or casual players, runs mixed-device or in-person sessions, or loses time helping returning players re-enter Foundry. Technically confident groups are negative controls.
rows.title: The likely TableStart payer is the table owner

rows.statement: The storefront proof can show a new player going from login to a correct current-turn action in under a minute, with the GM changing the permitted actions without editing many module settings. Test $10/$20/$30 against no purchase and a three-session pilot.
rows.title: TableStart has an eye-catching first-action demo

rows.statement: Hide UI controls per-player and global visibility; Player Pilot provides free mobile controls and common actions; Claim Your Hero handles character selection; Character Builder and Hero Mancer handle guided creation/level-up; AFK Ready Check handles readiness; SessionFlow sells a premium player workspace.
rows.title: Generic player simplification is already crowded

rows.statement: The official player orientation covers joining, claiming a character, understanding the interface, and moving on the map. A product must solve repeated context-specific table friction rather than repackage the basic tutorial.
rows.title: Foundry core already teaches the basic player path

rows.statement: A defensible product must combine GM-authored onboarding/return flow, current-beat context, role-specific permitted actions, completion/ready state, and safe fallback without becoming a second campaign workspace or system rules engine.
rows.title: The remaining TableStart wedge is a per-scene session recipe

rows.statement: A neutral record can carry a recipe, participant role, current beat, permitted action descriptors, linked actor/scene/document references, completion state, and fallback target. Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear require separate adapters for player, sheet, scene, and storage behavior.
rows.title: TableStart has a neutral session-recipe boundary but no VTT parity

rows.statement: Licensing risk is manageable if recipes use user-authored prompts and document references, but a player tutorial that bundles rulebook text, copyrighted examples, or copied adventure prose would create a separate content boundary.
rows.title: TableStart must store guidance and references rather than publisher text

rows.statement: The broad player-experience category is occupied or free; only a repeated onboarding or return-to-play failure that beats Hide UI plus Player Pilot/current setup at a non-zero price justifies further work.
rows.title: TableStart is conditional and fourth in the empirical queue

rows.statement: Recent table reports describe a GM display, shared TV or table screen, player phones/tablets, physical sheets/dice, and multiple browser clients, with setup, performance, player-view, and secret-visibility friction. This is a recruiting signal, not conversion evidence.
rows.title: In-person and hybrid Foundry tables have recurring multi-device coordination pain

rows.statement: A Foundry-first mode could register display/input roles, pair player controls, apply physical/digital dice policy, enforce secret-safe routing, reduce scene preload cost, show stale clients, and switch between in-person and remote profiles.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge is a fresh integrated table-mode challenger

rows.statement: The qualified payer runs at least two in-person or hybrid sessions per month and already owns a TV, projector, touchscreen, or player devices. Fully remote and paper-only tables are negative controls.
rows.title: The likely Tabletop Bridge payer is a recurring in-person or hybrid GM

rows.statement: The demo can show one GM screen, one clean shared map, two phone controls, and a physical d20 result applied to the same automated roll without exposing the GM view. Test $20/$35/$50 against no purchase and a three-session pilot.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge has an eye-catching multi-role demonstration

rows.statement: Monk's Common Display, Physical Play Dice, TouchVTT, Mobile Token Movement, Player Pilot, Gaming Table, Ninjo's In-Person Tools, and Lock View cover shared displays, physical rolls, touch, phone controls, paper/dice play, preload/display behavior, and view safety in separate combinations.
rows.title: Existing modules cover most Tabletop Bridge components

rows.statement: Ninjo's In-Person Tools advertises stopping player map downloads while retaining a usable canvas and supports both a following battlemap display and a pinned scene display. A new product must beat this current workflow rather than merely assemble the same features.
rows.title: Ninjo's In-Person Tools is a direct current integration anchor

rows.statement: The product must register display/input roles, validate secret-safe routing, detect stale or missing clients, apply a known scene/performance policy, and restore a weekly in-person/remote configuration. A feature bundle or repackage of existing modules is not sufficient.
rows.title: The remaining Tabletop Bridge wedge is orchestration and recovery

rows.statement: A neutral record can carry display roles, device capabilities, input policy, secret scope, scene policy, client status, and profile state. Roll20 and Owlbear expose different display, player, device, and dice-extension surfaces, so the record cannot establish equivalent orchestration.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge has a neutral table-session boundary but weak VTT portability

rows.statement: High-engagement in-person setup discussions and current module adoption establish a real workflow, but the components are mostly free or separately supported. Test $20/$35/$50 rather than inferring payment from use or hardware ownership.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge has use evidence but no product-specific payment evidence

rows.statement: The payer pool is narrower and the category is component-crowded. Only a measurable reduction in setup/recovery time that earns a non-zero price and a real-table pilot justifies further work.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge is conditional and fifth in the empirical queue

rows.statement: The current v14 package suppresses player map downloads, supports following and pinned display roles, rotates scenes, selects individual players, provides a touch-friendly sheet view and turn banner, and adds optional time/weather display.
rows.title: Ninjo's In-Person Tools closes most integrated table-mode features

rows.statement: Digital Tabletops is verified for Foundry 13â€“14 and adds controls for large displays while connecting to a free external IR-touch program. A new product cannot assume large-format or touch support is unserved.
rows.title: Digital Tabletops is a current large-format and IR-touch competitor

rows.statement: Table Mode supports a phone character sheet and movement controls but is PF2e-only, verified only for Foundry 13, and lists common-display support as planned. It is evidence of demand, not an open category by itself.
rows.title: Table Mode proves demand but is a narrow stale direct precedent

rows.statement: The only remaining theoretical wedge is cross-version/profile orchestration, stale-client and secret-routing health, recovery receipts, and compatibility management across a changing module stack. Existing display, touch, phone, and dice features should not be repackaged.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge would need paid reliability orchestration, not a feature bundle

rows.statement: High-engagement table setups and existing module use do not show a buyer paying for orchestration. Do not run the price/pilot arm until a paid alternative, named unsolved failure, or direct non-zero price signal is found.
rows.title: Tabletop Bridge has no product-specific payment evidence after current-package correction

rows.statement: DDB-Importer gates higher-value imports behind Patreon support, while historical R20Converter users paid for access and described the time saved as worth the fee. R20Converter later became public/free, so this is category and adoption evidence rather than current BridgeCheck WTP.
rows.title: Migration tools have observable category payment and adoption evidence

rows.statement: Community migration reports describe manual work, wall/light mismatches, missing or confusing imported content, importer setup friction, and substantial time savings when a converter works. Reports are source-specific and often older, so they justify a fixture rather than a universal failure claim.
rows.title: Campaign migration creates high-intent cleanup and deadline pain

rows.statement: A disposable target, source-to-target inventory, red/yellow/green receipt, link/asset/schema/permission checks, repair preview, and deterministic rerun could protect a migration without becoming another importer or redistributing source content.
rows.title: VTT BridgeCheck is a post-import assurance challenger

rows.statement: The highest-intent buyer is actively moving from Roll20, D&D Beyond, Fantasy Grounds, or another Foundry version/world, has significant imported content or a previous failure, and needs a playable target by a known date. Casual new-world creators are negative controls.
rows.title: The likely BridgeCheck payer is a GM with sunk campaign content and a migration deadline

rows.statement: The marketing proof can show a messy imported campaign producing counts of checked links/assets/permissions, flagged walls or unsupported fields, then a disposable repair and rerun with a clean receipt. Test one-time $10/$25/$50/$75 against no purchase.
rows.title: VTT BridgeCheck has a concrete receipt-based demo

rows.statement: DDB-Importer, VTTA, R20Converter, PDF-to-Foundry and official/premium content paths cover major source imports; Phils Map Migrator handles precise scene transfer; Foundry provides package compatibility and migration metadata.
rows.title: Source-specific importers already occupy the broad migration category

rows.statement: A defensible product compares source intent with target resolvability, exposes missing assets, broken links, geometry/schema/permission drift, and unsupported fields in a disposable rehearsal. A generic importer or source parser should be rejected.
rows.title: The remaining BridgeCheck wedge is source-neutral post-import verification

rows.statement: The product can inspect user-provided exports and target worlds, retain identifiers/fingerprints/check results, and preview repairs, but must not scrape source sites, bypass access controls, or redistribute rulebook/adventure text or assets.
rows.title: BridgeCheck must use user-owned exports and references without copying publisher content

rows.statement: A neutral receipt can carry source/target IDs, document kinds, asset fingerprints, link edges, schema versions, permission scopes, checks, repairs, and review decisions. Roll20, D&D Beyond, Fantasy Grounds, Owlbear, and Foundry have different export/API/storage semantics.
rows.title: BridgeCheck portability requires separate source and target adapters

rows.statement: The category has stronger payment evidence but migration is episodic and the exact importer may be good enough. The candidate advances only if migrating GMs choose a non-zero price after a named failure and complete two real pilots with a safe deterministic fixture.
rows.title: VTT BridgeCheck is conditional and sixth in the empirical queue

rows.statement: Recent requests ask for simpler loot distribution, shops, and adding items to player inventories; bulk loot and price creation are also described as tedious. This is a recruiting signal for ordinary campaign tables, not product-specific conversion evidence.
rows.title: Loot and party-economy transactions create recurring table friction

rows.statement: A player-first surface could route loot claims, approvals, shared currency, shop carts, sell-back, and auditable history while leaving the GM in control. A neutral party-ledger record could later render through multiple VTT adapters.
rows.title: LootFlow is a player-facing party-economy challenger

rows.statement: Item Piles covers loot piles, containers, merchants, and trading; Quartermaster covers shared party inventory/currency/history; Backpack covers storage; RPGX packages cover shops and shared economies; The Stockpile covers group carts, pooled funds, splitting, negotiation, sell-back, restock, services, and a ledger.
rows.title: Current Foundry packages already cover most LootFlow components

rows.statement: The remaining theoretical wedge is a cross-VTT, player-owned, conflict-safe transaction ledger with approvals, idempotent transfer, reconnect handling, and rollback. Current evidence does not show that buyers pay for this over Item Piles, Quartermaster, a free chest, or a hosted campaign tool.
rows.title: A prettier shop or generic party inventory is not a defensible LootFlow gap

rows.statement: An item/claim/currency/approval/transaction record can be shared, but item schemas, currency systems, permissions, offline behavior, and shop APIs differ across Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear. A second-VTT adapter would need explicit unsupported fields.
rows.title: LootFlow portability is a neutral ledger hypothesis, not VTT parity

rows.statement: The broad category is crowded and product-specific willingness to pay is absent. Revive only if a qualified GM names a repeated failure, chooses a non-zero price, and completes a three-session pilot against the exact current stack.
rows.title: LootFlow is rejected as a seventh challenger and negative control

rows.statement: Community requests ask for tracking actions, bonus actions, reactions, movement, and action budgets, while current descriptions explicitly target players forgetting what they have spent. This supports recruiting a table, not product-specific conversion.
rows.title: Combat action-budget confusion is a recurring player and GM friction signal

rows.statement: A minimal private turn card could show the active user remaining budget, usable actions, resource/reaction reminders, and a safe undo trail without becoming a full rules engine. A neutral action-ledger record could support later adapters.
rows.title: TurnReady is a player-facing combat-focus challenger

rows.statement: Action Keeper is current for v14 and tracks main/bonus/reaction/movement; Reaction Tracker is current through v14 for D&D 5e; Stylish Action HUD is a paid/patron v13-v14 HUD with actions/resources; PF2e Combater is a v14 turn planner with action budgets, execution, and undo; Argon, Token Action HUD, and system tools add more overlap.
rows.title: Current Foundry packages cover the broad action-budget and HUD surface

rows.statement: A paid HUD and premium combat products show that some tables pay for a better combat surface, but do not prove willingness to pay for another tracker. A minimal accessibility-first card must beat the exact current stack behaviorally.
rows.title: Combat HUD payment evidence is category evidence only

rows.statement: A neutral ledger can serialize actor, turn, resource, action, scope, reset, and undo state, but remaining actions, reactions, movement, sustain, MAP, and safe reversal depend on each game system and VTT permission model.
rows.title: TurnReady portability requires system-specific action semantics

rows.statement: The broad tracker/HUD category is crowded and product-specific WTP is absent. Revive only if a qualified table names a repeated accessibility or interruption failure, chooses a non-zero price, and completes a three-session pilot.
rows.title: TurnReady is rejected as an eighth challenger and negative control

rows.statement: A paid importer, HUD, Patreon product, or competitor subscription can prove that a category has spend, but it does not prove willingness to pay for a different wedge. Each candidate needs its own price choice, exact-alternative comparison, and pilot.
rows.title: Category payment evidence must not be transferred between candidates

rows.statement: Migration has a deadline-driven buyer and stronger observed category payment than the other current feature candidates, while the exact importer may still be sufficient. The first test must be importer-plus-cleanup versus assurance, not a generic converter demo.
rows.title: VTT BridgeCheck is first in the empirical queue

rows.statement: Update/recovery incidents can have high value for long-running module-heavy worlds, but product-specific payment evidence is weak and false-green/runtime risk is high.
rows.title: World Doctor is second in the empirical queue

rows.statement: It has recurring session lookup pain and a strong demo, but maintained free search, campaign tools, and AI alternatives make product-specific price choice essential.
rows.title: Adventure Navigator is third in the empirical queue

rows.statement: It has the strongest visual improvisation demo among the active arms, but MapForge and map-authoring tools are mandatory incumbents and asset rights remain a risk.
rows.title: Rapid Encounter Board is fourth in the empirical queue

rows.statement: Player onboarding pain is mixed and free UI/player-control tools are close substitutes; only a named new or returning-player failure should count.
rows.title: TableStart is fifth in the empirical queue

rows.statement: No candidate yet has product-specific WTP, two real pilots, runtime safety evidence, licensing clearance, and a cross-VTT result. Implementation remains paused.
rows.title: The current scorecard selects a buyer sequence, not a product

rows.statement: Foundry package metadata and primary document statistics include compatibility and modification information useful for auditing; a read-only receipt can inspect a disposable world/backup without becoming a live mutation tool.
rows.title: Foundry exposes a plausible local BridgeCheck evidence boundary

rows.statement: Official backup guidance says package backups and snapshots do not include assets outside the package directories. This creates a concrete missing-file/reference verification job, but does not prove buyers will pay for it.
rows.title: Foundry backups do not fully verify or preserve external assets

rows.statement: Without the user's authentication token, DDB-Importer is restricted to public information; the token is sensitive and must not be shared with another product.
rows.title: DDB-Importer relies on user authentication for private D&D Beyond data

rows.statement: Basic character/spell/item/adventure functions are available without Patreon, while some higher-value imports require Patreon support or a user-run proxy. This is category/payment evidence, not BridgeCheck WTP.
rows.title: DDB-Importer has a visible paid/proxy boundary

rows.statement: Synthetic or user-owned documents can exercise versions, assets, scenes, geometry, links, ownership, missing files, duplicates, unsupported fields, reruns, and repair previews while leaving the live world untouched.
rows.title: The first BridgeCheck fixture must be Foundry-local and disposable

rows.statement: Roll20 documents Character Vault and Pro Transmogrifier workflows for moving characters, maps, tokens, handouts, macros, and other objects between Roll20 games. This does not establish a general external export API for BridgeCheck.
rows.title: Roll20's documented transfer surface is primarily intra-platform

rows.statement: Owlbear extensions can store namespaced metadata on scenes/items/players, read permissions, download scenes/assets, and use room metadata, but room metadata is limited to 16 kB.
rows.title: Owlbear supports compact extension metadata rather than full campaign transfer

rows.statement: The portable record should contain IDs, document kinds, asset fingerprints, links, schema/version data, permission scopes, check states, unsupported fields, repair proposals, and review decisions, not copied publisher text/assets or live-VTT parity.
rows.title: The portable BridgeCheck artifact is a versioned receipt contract

rows.statement: Roll20 requires a supplied inventory/copy boundary, while Owlbear can render a compact receipt through an extension. Separate adapters can be tested after Foundry proof without account impersonation or scraping.
rows.title: A second-VTT BridgeCheck adapter must be user-mediated and read-only at first

rows.statement: The technical audit supports a Foundry post-import assurance product, not a universal converter. Reject if the local fixture cannot identify real failures without copying content or if the exact importer/manual path wins every price test.
rows.title: BridgeCheck remains first in the queue but has a narrower go/no-go promise

rows.statement: A recent Pathfinder 2e discussion describes players still losing time after nine months because sheet tabs, icons, and controls remain hard to locate. This is a recurring session-friction signal, not product WTP.
rows.title: Player confusion can persist after months of Foundry use

rows.statement: Foundry reports D&D 5e at 64.28% of installed systems, PF2e at 30.52%, an average of 37.44 installed modules, and 33% of users owning premium content. This indicates reach and category spending, not Player Compass WTP.
rows.title: Foundry has a large D&D/PF2e audience and observable premium category spending

rows.statement: Foundry Navigator supports keyboard-first and screen-reader-friendly D&D 5e navigation; Token Action HUD, PF2e HUD, Argon, Stylish Action HUD, Hide UI, and system sheets cover direct actions, visibility, and UI simplification.
rows.title: Current HUD and accessibility tools close the broad player-surface gap

rows.statement: An automatic per-player surface could select the current exploration, social, or combat context and present the next relevant actions in plain language without replacing the native sheet.
rows.title: Player Compass is a fresh recurring-use challenger

rows.statement: Another action bar or sheet skin is crowded. The remaining hypothesis is a system-aware, read-only capability surface that explains why an action is available and adapts to session context, keyboard use, low resolution, and screen readers.
rows.title: The defensible Player Compass wedge is automatic context selection with near-zero GM setup

rows.statement: The likely buyer runs tables with returning, low-confidence, accessibility-needing, or mixed-experience players; the player benefits daily but usually does not control the module purchase.
rows.title: Player Compass payer is a GM or host with recurring player friction

rows.statement: The demo can show a cluttered sheet collapsing to one focused â€œwhat can I do now?â€ card, then switching context without manual scene recipes. Test $10/$20/$30/$39/no purchase.
rows.title: Player Compass has an immediate before-and-after demo

rows.statement: A portable record can describe capability IDs, labels, context, visibility, prerequisites, and supported actions, but each VTT/system must supply its own read-only adapter and semantics.
rows.title: Player Compass portability is a neutral capability manifest, not shared rules logic

rows.statement: Stylish Action HUD, SessionFlow, and Originate currently sell or gate polished player/GM interface experiences through publisher or premium access. This validates category spending, not Player Compass conversion.
rows.title: Premium visual and player-facing UX is an observed Foundry payment category

rows.statement: A player-facing context surface could be used during ordinary play whenever a player chooses an action, while BridgeCheck is used around a migration and World Doctor around an incident. Frequency is a marketability proxy, not WTP.
rows.title: Player Compass has higher routine frequency than migration assurance

rows.statement: Stylish Action HUD and current free/system HUDs already cover direct action access, party display, and visual polish. Only automatic context selection, plain-language explanation, accessibility, and near-zero GM setup remain unproven.
rows.title: Premium HUD payment does not leave a broad Player Compass gap

rows.statement: Migration deadlines and importer payment make BridgeCheck a credible buyer test, but a successful importer or manual cleanup may eliminate repeat demand.
rows.title: BridgeCheck retains urgency and a strong payment proxy but is episodic

rows.statement: Recurring use plus a visible premium UX category gives it the best current marketability hypothesis, but exact-HUD preference, non-zero price, pilots, runtime safety, and portability remain unproven.
rows.title: Player Compass moves to the first empirical gate without being selected

rows.statement: Public responses describe the subscription as worth it, say the creator is rapidly improving the module, report that players love it, and express immediate willingness to pay for additional system support. This is incumbent behavioral evidence, not Player Compass WTP.
rows.title: Stylish Action HUD has explicit public payment-intent and satisfaction signals

rows.statement: The incumbent is a visual-only overlay that triggers standard system rolls and supports minimal mode, while current HUDs provide direct actions. Player Compass cannot compete on animation or action access alone; its remaining claim is automatic context selection and explanation.
rows.title: Stylish Action HUD leaves only a narrow Player Compass gap

rows.statement: Public responses include requests for only HP/minimal information, criticism that visual effects become annoying, and rejection of AI-linked paid access. A product offer must support quiet/minimal mode and test one-time pricing separately.
rows.title: Some buyers reject forced cinematic style or subscriptions

rows.statement: A broader payment discussion identifies ready-to-run maps, scenes, assets, automation helpers, and reusable effects as paid value, usually through creator memberships. This validates the ecosystem, not a new utility module.
rows.title: Foundry buyers publicly describe prepared content and reusable helpers as worth paying for

rows.statement: The incumbent already converts visual presentation and direct actions. The new offer must show a player finding the next valid action with no GM-built recipe, preserve user choice, and avoid a subscription assumption.
rows.title: Player Compass should sell zero-setup clarity rather than a prettier HUD

rows.statement: Players can target and roll against an enemy, but Foundry permissions prevent them from applying damage or effects to tokens they do not own. Recent reports describe the repeated target re-selection and GM confirmation as a frustrating multi-step workflow.
rows.title: Foundry forces the GM to mirror clear player intent for unowned targets

rows.statement: Community users describe target-aware buttons that reduce the workflow to one GM confirmation as a major timesaver, while newer reports still encounter the native wrong-target behavior. This establishes pain and demo value, not WTP.
rows.title: A one-click GM confirmation is a visible relief for target-resolution friction

rows.statement: D&D 5e Effective Tray NG can relay damage or effects to unowned targets through an active GM client, PF2e Toolbelt provides target-aware application, PF2e Saves Helper provides current per-target and bulk buttons, and older Damage Application is stale. No single current package establishes a portable, system-agnostic handoff product.
rows.title: Current resolution substitutes are fragmented by system and trust model

rows.statement: The candidate should emit a player intent envelope and give the GM an accept, adjust, reject, expire, or undo decision. The player must not gain unowned-token write access and hidden defenses must not be disclosed.
rows.title: Resolve Relay should preserve GM authority instead of bypassing permissions

rows.statement: Actor, target, requested operation, roll result, and visible explanation can form a neutral protocol. Damage mitigation, conditions, hidden data, target identity, and final mutation still require a Foundry/system adapter and cannot be promised across VTTs from static evidence.
rows.title: A neutral action envelope is portable, but rules resolution is not

rows.statement: The repeated value is saved GM attention and fewer wrong-target corrections during every combat, while players are the beneficiaries. A buyer test must target GMs running D&D 5e or PF2e rather than infer individual-player payment.
rows.title: The likely payer for Resolve Relay is the combat-heavy GM or host

rows.statement: Current PF2e Toolbelt, PF2e Saves Helper, and D&D5e Effective Tray NG cover most of the target-aware resolution workflow. Community pain establishes usefulness, but payment for a new confirmation layer remains unproven.
rows.title: Resolve Relay proposed paid gap is closed by current free target-aware modules

rows.statement: Intent envelopes, stale-request expiry, and idempotent undo are useful implementation patterns, but cross-system support and safety review weaken a paid case when current tools solve the named workflow.
rows.title: Resolve Relay should remain a reusable protocol asset rather than the next buyer gate

rows.statement: Payment for broader NPC automation or presentation suites is a category signal only. It does not establish buyer demand for the smaller Resolve Relay handoff.
rows.title: Premium combat automation does not transfer willingness to pay to a confirmation layer

rows.statement: Official Foundry guidance identifies port-forwarding frustration, CGNAT, router-behind-router failures, and network configuration as barriers to self-hosting. Current community reports add changing ISP support, stale tunnels, and failed player joins.
rows.title: Self-hosted Foundry connectivity is a recurring GM failure point

rows.statement: Molten advertises plans starting at four dollars per month and The Forge sells a turn-key hosted experience. This anchors category spending but does not prove TableLink willingness to pay.
rows.title: Foundry hosting partners establish a real recurring payment anchor

rows.statement: Foundry Tunnel Manager, Cloudflare, ngrok, playit.gg, Tailscale, ZeroTier, VPNs, Molten, and The Forge cover pieces of reachability or hosting. Their presence makes a generic tunnel a weak product boundary.
rows.title: Tunnel and hosting alternatives solve fragments while leaving setup and diagnostics fragmented

rows.statement: The candidate should provide provider-neutral preflight, external join verification, websocket and heartbeat monitoring, reconnect, stale-link warnings, player-safe diagnostics, and explicit fallback while preserving local world files.
rows.title: TableLink wedge is game-night reliability rather than another tunnel

rows.statement: Foundry is the first implementation target. A neutral gateway contract may later support another browser VTT, but provider APIs, authentication, token semantics, and hosting behavior require separate adapters.
rows.title: A local HTTP and WebSocket gateway is transport-portable but provider and auth adapters are not

rows.statement: The strongest test segment combines recurring sessions, a recent player-join or network failure, reluctance to pay recurring hosting fees, or a need for a local emergency fallback. Compare both DIY and paid-host cohorts.
rows.title: TableLink payer is a recurring self-hosting GM with connectivity trouble and local-data preference

rows.statement: Short-lived invite tokens, explicit local bind and port approval, no bundled or resold provider credentials, no game-content inspection, and a local audit log are required boundaries for a trustworthy gateway.
rows.title: TableLink must use user-mediated provider accounts and avoid game-payload inspection

rows.statement: The current open-source utility supports Windows CLI and desktop releases, multiple tunnel providers, start and stop, logs, URL copying, a local dashboard, WebSocket live status, and notifications when a tunnel dies or is about to expire.
rows.title: Foundry Tunnel Manager materially closes the generic TableLink gateway gap

rows.statement: A new provider wrapper or dashboard would duplicate a current free utility and the underlying tunnel providers. The remaining candidate must verify the user-facing session path rather than manage another tunnel.
rows.title: Generic TableLink gateway management is not a defensible paid wedge

rows.statement: The narrowed product checks the exact player invite from an independent vantage, confirms expected Foundry HTTP and WebSocket behavior, records a safe health receipt, detects stale or mismatched links, and returns a green or red send decision without replacing the tunnel or host.
rows.title: JoinProof / Game Night Gatekeeper is a pre-session invitation verifier

rows.statement: Foundry documentation and current community reports establish connection setup and failure pain, yet the GM may only experience it episodically and may accept a phone or player check for free.
rows.title: A player-join failure can be catastrophic immediately before a session, but buyer frequency is unproven

rows.statement: Molten, The Forge, and other hosts remove much of the network setup and reliability burden for a recurring fee. Their prices anchor category spending while also shrinking the independent verifier buyer segment.
rows.title: Managed hosting directly substitutes for a self-hosting verifier

rows.statement: A neutral receipt can contain URL, TLS, HTTP status, WebSocket reachability, latency, timestamp, and expiry, but VTT authentication and session semantics require separate adapters and no parity claim.
rows.title: A health receipt is more portable than a gateway implementation

rows.statement: A same-network check can pass because of NAT loopback while players fail externally. A trustworthy test therefore needs a user-mediated remote player or a small independent probe, creating recurring infrastructure, abuse, privacy, and availability costs.
rows.title: Independent external verification requires a remote device or service

rows.statement: The verifier should use only user-authorized invite and protocol checks, retain minimal local receipts, avoid login capture and game-content inspection, and never silently alter bind, port, provider, or access settings.
rows.title: JoinProof must not collect credentials or game payloads

rows.statement: Foundry tutorial material describes a remote-host yes or no test for the invitation link. A standalone generic external reachability product must add materially more than an up or down signal.
rows.title: Foundry core already performs a remote connectivity check

rows.statement: UptimeRobot provides free HTTP, port, ping, keyword, API, and related monitoring, while Uptime Kuma supports HTTP, TCP, WebSocket, ping, DNS, and other self-hosted monitors.
rows.title: Generic HTTP, port, keyword, and WebSocket monitoring is already widely available

rows.statement: A defensible wedge would identify the expected world or session, distinguish stale or wrong endpoints, exercise the intended login or user-seat path without credentials, and explain the player-facing result.
rows.title: JoinProof would need Foundry-semantic session verification to escape generic monitoring

rows.statement: Same-network checks can pass through NAT loopback while external players fail. A remote device or probe service is required for confidence and introduces availability, abuse, privacy, and operating-cost risk.
rows.title: Independent probing creates recurring service and false-green costs

rows.statement: Foundry, FTM, generic monitors, and a player or phone test may be good enough. No standalone verifier should be built without product-specific failure and payment evidence.
rows.title: JoinProof should remain a negative control until a named false-green failure survives existing checks

rows.statement: Community reports describe repeated scheduling friction, late replies, cancellations, and campaigns failing to reach the next session. This is a recruiting signal, not a conversion rate.
rows.title: Recurring campaigns lose momentum when availability and quorum remain uncertain

rows.statement: Doodle supplies polls, deadlines, reminders, participant tracking, calendar invites, and integrations; Discord Events provide RSVP and notifications; Warhorn handles gaming event registration.
rows.title: Doodle, Discord Events, and Warhorn cover much of group scheduling and attendance

rows.statement: Foundry can display a next session date, World & Campaign Builder covers session planning and tracking, and SessionFlow provides a premium GM/player session workspace. The gap is not another calendar or planning canvas.
rows.title: Foundry offers a next-session field while current campaign tools cover planning and live tracking

rows.statement: The candidate would collect availability, show green/yellow/red quorum, send a deadline and reminder, freeze the roster, and make run, reschedule, recruit, or prepared fallback actions explicit.
rows.title: Session Pulse should sell consequence-aware quorum and fallback

rows.statement: Players benefit from clarity, but the person paying is most likely the GM or event organizer who loses prep time and campaign momentum. Ordinary groups remain the required baseline control.
rows.title: Session Pulse payer is likely a recurring GM, paid GM, or organized-play coordinator

rows.statement: A neutral event and attendance contract can work across browser VTTs, while Discord, calendar, email, and player identity adapters require separate consent and platform handling.
rows.title: Attendance and event records are portable but notification integrations are not

rows.statement: Doodle offers a free baseline and a Professional plan around fifteen dollars per month in the United States with deadlines, automated reminders, participant tracking, hidden details, and calendar synchronization. This proves category payment, not Session Pulse conversion.
rows.title: Doodle charges for coordination features that overlap Session Pulse

rows.statement: An ordinary group can use a free poll, a Discord RSVP event, a shared calendar, or a message thread without buying a Foundry product.
rows.title: Free Doodle, Discord Events, and group messages remain strong controls for ordinary campaigns

rows.statement: The paid promise is turning an uncertain session into a documented run, reschedule, recruit, or fallback decision before the GM invests more prep. A better poll is not enough.
rows.title: Session Pulse must sell avoided prep loss and a quorum decision rather than scheduling

rows.statement: The person paying may be an event organizer or paid GM who directly loses revenue or prep time, while an ordinary home campaign may reject all paid coordination. Pooled WTP would overstate market size.
rows.title: Ordinary groups, paid GMs, and organized-play coordinators must be measured separately

rows.statement: A local attendance utility could be sold once, but hosted reminders, Discord/calendar integrations, and notification delivery create continuing service and API costs. Test $10/$20/$39/no purchase separately from $3/$5/month/no recurring fee.
rows.title: Session Pulse needs separate buy-once and maintenance price tests

rows.statement: Category spending is meaningful only when a qualified GM prefers the consequence-aware Foundry workflow over the exact free stack and commits to repeated use.
rows.title: Doodle payment cannot be transferred to Session Pulse without a named prep-loss incident

rows.statement: Recent community reports describe four to five hours of preparation for a three-hour session, extensive context switching, and repeated frustration when carefully prepared material is ignored. These are anecdotal buyer-pain signals, not conversion rates.
rows.title: Recurring GM prep burden is a strong recruiting signal

rows.statement: SessionFlow, World & Campaign Builder, RPGM Forge, current AI/prep tools, and Foundry premium content occupy campaign planning, live widgets, player panels, content generation, or ready-made preparation.
rows.title: Current premium and free prep suites close the broad GM-prep category

rows.statement: The remaining narrow hypothesis is to recover unused scenes, NPCs, promises, or encounters when players pivot, while preserving permissions, provenance, and publisher-content boundaries. More canvas or generated content is not enough.
rows.title: A new prep product would need safe reuse of discarded preparation rather than another workspace

rows.statement: Player Compass combines recurring use with a visible premium UX category, while BridgeCheck retains migration urgency and World Doctor retains long-running incident value. No candidate has product-specific WTP yet.
rows.title: Player Compass remains the first empirical gate after the recurring-prep scan

rows.statement: Fresh prep pain does not justify opening another broad product because exact current tools and free alternatives remain strong. Reopen only for a named pivot or prep-loss failure with non-zero price evidence.
rows.title: Generic prep workspace, generic AI prep, and generic session scheduling remain negative controls

rows.statement: D&D5e and PF2e expose different action semantics, permissions, sheet controls, and content surfaces. A safe product asks each system adapter what it can describe instead of becoming a universal rules engine.
rows.title: Player Compass must use separate system adapters and a neutral capability manifest

rows.statement: Foundry Navigator covers keyboard and screen-reader navigation plus target, damage, healing, focus, and low-resolution workflows; Token Action HUD provides direct D&D5e rolls and item use; PF2e HUD is current for PF2e and Starfinder 2e.
rows.title: Foundry Navigator, Token Action HUD D&D5e, and PF2e HUD close the broad action-access promise

rows.statement: The product must explain what is relevant now and why, preserve the native sheet and exact HUD stack, and keep every action user-invoked without hidden writes or a replacement rules engine.
rows.title: The remaining Player Compass wedge is zero-setup, read-only context explanation
